source_document.body:
Mexican manufacturers produced 15,181 heavy-duty vehicles during September, compared with 6,857 in the same month last year.
Exports totaled 12,707 units, up 144.6% from September 2025, marking a significant acceleration in cross-border commercial vehicle shipments, according to figures from Mexico’s National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI) presented by the National Association of Bus, Truck and Tractor-Trailer Producers (ANPACT).
The September rebound comes as Mexico’s domestic heavy-duty vehicle market continues to struggle with weak sales , delayed fleet replacement decisions and uncertainty surrounding U.S. trade policies.
Rogelio Arzate, executive president of ANPACT, said growing demand from U.S. customers preparing for new emissions standards has been a major factor behind the increase in production and exports.
“The reason why production and exports are growing at the levels they are is precisely because the United States, our main trading partner, is currently undergoing this technology shift,” Arzate said during an October news conference .
Arzate pointed to the transition toward U.S. Environmental Protection Agency emissions standards scheduled for 2027, which is prompting manufacturers and customers to adjust their purchasing and production plans.
“Clients are currently requesting a significant number of units as well, and that is why this production and export toward the United States is increasing,” Arzate said.
The growth highlights Mexico’s role as a major production hub for commercial trucks sold throughout North America, even as manufacturers navigate tariffs , evolving emissions requirements and the upcoming review of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement.
Sources: INEGI, Registro Administrativo de la Industria Automotriz de Vehículos Pesados, Oct. 9, 2026; ANPACT-AMDA October 2026 news conference transcript.
US remains Mexico’s largest heavy-duty truck export market
Mexico exported 98,394 heavy-duty vehicles during the first nine months of 2026, an increase of approximately 12% compared with the same period last year, according to ANPACT.
Of those shipments, 98,389 were freight vehicles, representing a 12.1% year-over-year increase.
The U.S. remained the industry’s dominant export destination, receiving 90,967 Mexican-built heavy-duty vehicles from January through September, up 9.6% from the comparable 2025 period.
That means the U.S. accounted for approximately 92.5% of Mexico’s heavy-duty vehicle exports during the first nine months of the year.
Canada also recorded gains, with shipments increasing 47.6% year over year through September. During September alone, Mexico exported 680 heavy-duty vehicles to Canada, more than doubling the volume recorded a year earlier.
Other markets showing year-to-date growth included Colombia, Peru, Honduras and Guatemala, while exports to Chile, El Salvador, Ecuador and Costa Rica declined.
The export gains accompanied a broader recovery in Mexican commercial vehicle manufacturing.
During the January-through-September period, Mexican factories produced 117,121 heavy-duty vehicles, an increase of 10.3% from the same period in 2025.
Freight vehicles accounted for 114,443 units of that production.
Diesel-powered vehicles continued to dominate the industry’s manufacturing and export activity. ANPACT reported no electric or natural gas-powered heavy-duty vehicles produced or exported during September.
Domestic truck sales continue to struggle
Despite stronger manufacturing and export activity, Mexico’s domestic heavy-duty vehicle market remained under pressure.
Cristina Vázquez, coordinator of economic studies at the Mexican Association of Automotive Distributors (AMDA), said retail sales totaled 2,980 heavy-duty vehicles in September, down 11.3% from the same month in 2025.
The decline marked the eighth consecutive month of year-over-year decreases in Mexico’s heavy-duty vehicle retail market.
Through the first nine months of 2026, retail sales totaled 25,289 vehicles, a 17.5% decline from the comparable period last year.
Sales of tractor-trailers were particularly weak.
Mexican dealers sold 1,153 tractor-trucks during September, down 14% year over year. Sales of other freight trucks increased slightly, rising 0.5% to 1,378 units.
Combined, the freight vehicle segment recorded 2,531 retail sales, down 6.7% from September 2025.
Passenger vehicle sales, including buses, fell 30.5% to 449 units.
Vázquez said Mexico’s commercial vehicle market has yet to recover from a surge in purchases during 2024, when fleet operators accelerated acquisitions ahead of regulatory changes.
The record sales that year effectively pulled forward demand that otherwise might have occurred in 2025 and 2026.
She also cited uncertainty surrounding U.S. trade policies and the upcoming USMCA review as factors discouraging fleet operators from making major investments.
The market’s continued weakness comes despite signs of improvement in Mexico’s broader economy, including a rebound in fixed investment.
AMDA projected annual heavy-duty vehicle retail sales of approximately 36,051 units in 2026 but cautioned that actual results could fall below that estimate if purchasing activity remains subdued.
ANPACT pushes for tariff relief, fleet renewal programs
Arzate said ANPACT is working with Mexican authorities to address U.S. tariffs on commercial vehicles and components as the North American automotive industry prepares for the USMCA review.
The association is seeking lower tariffs and wants to preserve existing regional rules of origin, which require manufacturers to meet increasing North American content thresholds.
Arzate said manufacturers have made substantial investments in their supply chains and production facilities to comply with the agreement.
He said the industry’s preferred outcome would be eliminating U.S. tariffs imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act, although reducing those duties may be a more achievable near-term goal.
“In an ideal world, we should have zero tariffs,” Arzate said.
ANPACT is also working with Mexico’s Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Economy on programs aimed at encouraging domestic fleet replacement.
The initiatives include accelerated depreciation, financing guarantees and a proposed scrappage program designed to remove older commercial vehicles from service.
Arzate said the association is coordinating with Nacional Financiera, Mexico’s development bank, on additional financial incentives to help carriers purchase newer equipment.

source_document.body:
Jim Himes, ranking member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence addresses the Warsaw Security Conference (Warsaw Security Conference)
BELFAST — The pace of US military aid to Ukraine is likely to ramp up if Democrats win control of the House of Representatives and Senate in November’s midterm elections, according to the top Democrat on the House’s intelligence committee.
A switch in power “does change things,” Connecticut Rep. Jim Himes, ranking member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, said today at the Warsaw Security Conference .
“It means that aid packages [to Ukraine] move not in nine months, but in nine days or nine weeks on the outside, and that the message [of support to Ukraine] is very different,” he said.
Himes comments come amid reports that the Trump administration has threatened to stifle the procurement system supplying weapons to Ukraine in a bid to pressure Kyiv into ending deep strikes against Russian energy infrastructure. On Sunday, US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia. He has also received bipartisan criticism for temporarily lifting restrictions on Russian diesel exports.
Under NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, NATO allies and partners fund the purchase of US-sourced weapons and equipment for Ukraine, with NATO coordinating deliveries. The mechanism depends on Washington making those weapons available for purchase, meaning the Trump administration could still affect the flow of European-funded military assistance by restricting access to US equipment.
If Democrats gain control of both chambers and the budget, Trump could be forced to negotiate with the party to fund his priorities, Himes said. In exchange for accepting those terms, Democrats would “demand” that the president adopts a “much more affirmative and consistent policy in support of Ukraine.”
Himes said polling and prediction markets suggest the midterms could deliver “a fairly massive repudiation of the president,” though he argued that the result would not be driven directly by Trump’s Russia-Ukraine policy.
“It will be because, in a remarkable political experiment,” Trump said he would not go to war in the Middle East and would lower living costs, he said.
“And he did precisely the opposite of both those things,” Himes said. “What happens in November is going to be almost certainly a switch of control in the House of Representatives, and quite likely a switch of control in the Senate.”
Speaking in Warsaw on Monday, Mississippi Sen. Roger Wicker, chair of the Senate Committee on Armed Services, deferred to NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe Gen. Alexus Grynkewich , when offering thoughts on Ukraine and Iran.
Grynkewich “thinks we’re up to the task with regard to helping Ukraine and finishing whatever the President [Trump] intends to do after the election in Iran,” Wicker explained. “My viewpoint, and I’ve expressed this publicly and told the president, my viewpoint is that the memorandum of understanding and stopping and starting [peace negotiations] was not a good idea with regard to Iran.”

Posted By: Blair McBride October 13, 2026
SSR Mining (TSX, Nasdaq: SSRM) agreed to buy Nevada-focused explorer Roxmore Resources (TSX: RM) for $464 million (C$660.1 million) as it released an updated report for the nearby Marigold mine that raises its life to 20 years.
The all-cash deal would give SSR Roxmore’s Converse project, located just 6 km west of the producing Marigold mine, potentially adding 150,000 to 170,000 oz. of annual gold production over a 10-year life. Converse is about 275 km northeast of Nevada’s capital, Carson City.
Expanding production profile
“This transaction [is] positive for SSRM shares, as it secures a large, adjacent development asset that can materially extend and expand [SSR’s] U.S. production profile while leveraging the existing Marigold infrastructure and operating platform,” Scotia Capital analyst Ovais Habib said in a note on Tuesday.
“This acquisition appears consistent with management’s low-capital-intensity growth strategy and is expected to be accretive to net asset value and mineral resources.”
The deal represents a “compelling opportunity” to add a high-quality gold resource near Marigold at a good valuation, SSR Executive Chairman Rod Antal said in a release.
“We have been carefully monitoring the progress of the Converse deposit for some time, and have conducted a focused due diligence review of the asset,” he said. “SSR Mining is the natural acquiror of this exciting deposit and developing an asset in close proximity to Marigold will allow for clear operating and financial efficiencies.”
The deal would strengthen SSR’s position among the largest U.S. gold producers while advancing its strategy of building a long-term production hub in Nevada. It also comes about six months after SSR sold its 80% stake in Turkey’s Çöpler mine , where the company suspended operations in 2024 following a heap-leach pad landslide that killed nine miners.
SSR shares down
Despite the announced deal, SSR shares fell 7% to $46.72 apiece on Tuesday morning in Toronto, possibly due to the relatively high initial costs at Converse of $829 million, according to an April 2026 preliminary economic assessment (PEA). SSR has a market capitalization of about $9.4 billion. The stock has traded in a 12-month range of $25.83 to $54.50. Roxmore shares surged 30% to a new 52-week high of $6.96 each, for a market value of $502.1 million.
Discounted at 5%, Converse has a post-tax net present value (NPV) of $2.7 billion, assuming a consensus gold price of $3,600 per oz., and a post-tax internal rate of return (IRR) of 42.8%, according to the PEA. The open-pit Converse could produce 250,000 oz. annually over a 15-year life.
Converse hosts 103 million indicated tonnes grading 0.65 gram gold per tonne for 2.2 million contained oz. 218 million inferred tonnes at 0.43 gram gold for 3 million oz., according to a March resource update.
Once the project begins output, SSR’s annual production profile in the United States could exceed 450,000 oz. during peak years. It would average about 350,000 to 400,000 oz. from 2033 to 2042, SSR said. The company’s other U.S. mine is Cripple Creek & Victor , located in Colorado.
Marigold reserves boost
Meanwhile, SSR’s updated life-of-mine plan for Marigold raises its active mine life by five years to 20 years and its probable gold reserves by 43% to 4.6 million oz. over the previous estimate from 2025. Life-of-mine production grew 46% to 3.2 million ounces.
The report more than triples Marigold’s post-tax NPV to $3.3 billion, while life-of-mine capital costs more than tripled to $1.3 billion. It assumes a gold price of $3,948 per ounce.
The update incorporates the initial life of mine plan for the Buffalo Valley project with 700,000 oz. of probable reserves and first production expected in 2029. Buffalo Valley is 24 km southwest of the main Marigold mine.
Future production growth
Scotia Capital’s Habib said the report is positive for SSR, as the reserve increase extends Marigold’s mine life, improves long-term production visibility and shows value creation through reserve conversion.
“The incorporation of Buffalo Valley into the mine plan provides an additional source of future production growth, while [SSR’s] estimated after-tax NPV (…) underscores Marigold’s strategic importance within [SSR’s] increasingly attractive U.S.-focused asset base,” he said.
The updated report bolsters Marigold’s position as a top asset in the U.S., SSR’s Antal said.
“Over the next three years, we plan to invest in Marigold to modernize the operation for future success through fleet and heap leach pad expansions that aim to improve its operational flexibility and reliability,” he said.
The new plan highlights the growing importance of satellite deposits in extending the productive lives of established gold mines, allowing operators to leverage existing infrastructure rather than develop new mining complexes.

The SONAR Pricing Power Index (PPI) fell to 70 this week from 71, its fourth straight weekly decline, but freight carriers still hold the upper hand in rate negotiations. Softer intermodal contract rates and ocean import bookings drove the dip, while truckload tender rejections held steady near 13.9%.
On the PPI’s 0–100 scale, 50 represents a historically balanced market. A reading of 70 means pricing power continues to favor carriers over shippers heading into the fourth quarter.
Key takeaways: SONAR PPI, week of Oct. 12, 2026
PPI: 70 (down from 71). Fourth consecutive weekly decline, still firmly carrier-favorable.
Three-month outlook: 76 (down from 79). The model gave back most of last week’s gain but still expects carrier leverage to build into mid-January.
Capacity is steady. The national tender rejection rate (STRI) was 13.85%, in the 83rd percentile of the past five years.
Intermodal contract rates fell to $1.61 a mile from $1.68, the single biggest drag on the index.
Spot rates are holding near July levels. The national spot rate eased to $3.52 a mile from $3.56, still in the 95th percentile.
Rail volume remains elevated in the 99th percentile as truck-to-rail conversion continues.
What pulled the index lower
Two metrics accounted for most of this week’s decline. Intermodal contract rates dropped to the 36th percentile from the 54th, taking roughly 0.9 points off the score on their own. Ocean import bookings slipped about 2% to the 48th percentile from the 56th, costing about 0.6 points. Small gains in van contract rates, the spot-contract spread, rejections and accepted volume clawed back about half a point.
Capacity: rejections hold in carrier territory
The national tender rejection rate was essentially flat at 13.85% versus 13.84% last week. Weekly rejections have stayed between roughly 13.3% and 14.4% since early August, well below the 17–18% peak of late June but still more than two and a half times the level of two years ago.
The full report explains why SONAR’s model expects rejections to move higher from here rather than hold at current levels.
Demand: rail stays strong, truckload volume stays soft
Rail volume eased less than 1% to 35,575 loaded containers but held in the 99th percentile. Truckload carriers continue to be more selective about the freight they accept, pushing loads onto rail on lanes of roughly 550 to 1,500 miles. Accepted truckload volume rose about 1% but remains near the bottom of its range, in the 13th percentile. Ocean import bookings softened yet are still running above last year’s levels.
Pricing: contract rates catching up to spot
Van contract rates ticked up to $2.74 a mile, moving to the 84th percentile, as carriers reprice contracts upward. The spot-contract spread narrowed to negative $0.11 from negative $0.15. It has been negative since mid-September because spot rates have pulled back from their early-July peak of $3.80 while contract rates keep rising.
What the three-month outlook signals
The three-month PPI outlook trimmed to 76 but remains well above today’s reading of 70. The model projects tender rejections reaching the 93rd percentile by mid-January, with spot rates and rail volume at the very top of their historical ranges. The full report breaks down the forecast metric by metric.

About the SONAR Pricing Power Index
The SONAR Pricing Power Index is a weekly composite score that measures whether carriers or shippers hold negotiating leverage in the U.S. freight market. It combines eight SONAR metrics (tender rejections, accepted volume, rail volume, ocean TEU bookings, spot rates, van contract rates, the spot/contract spread and intermodal contract rates), ranks each against its own five-year weekly history and weights them into a single score from 0 to 100. A 50 is a historically balanced market. Higher readings favor carriers; lower readings favor shippers.
Frequently asked questions
What is the SONAR Pricing Power Index (PPI)? The SONAR PPI is a weekly 0–100 score built from eight SONAR freight metrics that shows whether carriers or shippers hold pricing power. A 50 is balanced; above 50 favors carriers; below 50 favors shippers.
What is this week’s PPI reading? The SONAR PPI was 70 for the week of Oct. 12, 2026, down from 71 the prior week. It was the fourth consecutive weekly decline.
Why did the PPI decline this week? Intermodal contract rates fell to $1.61 a mile from $1.68 and ocean import bookings dropped about 2%. Together they subtracted roughly 1.5 points, partly offset by small gains elsewhere.
Do carriers or shippers have pricing power right now? Carriers. At 70, the PPI sits well above the balanced level of 50, supported by tender rejections near 13.9% and spot rates in the 95th percentile.
What is the PPI outlook for the next three months? The three-month outlook is 76, down from 79 last week. The model expects tender rejections to climb toward the 93rd percentile by mid-January.

Today’s threat environment is increasingly shaped by low-cost drones, high‑volume attacks that can overwhelm defenses, and diverse air and surface threats. In response, forces need munitions that adapt quickly across mission sets, are upgradable, dependable, and scalable.
BAE Systems’ APKWS laser-guidance kit continues to meet that need by turning widely available 70millimeter rockets into accurate, low‑collateral weapons for counter‑UAS, air‑to‑air, and multi‑mission roles across U.S. and allied forces. Recent operations and tests show units can move from evaluation to live missions rapidly, delivering intercepts at a fraction of the cost of traditional air‑to‑air missiles while providing a cost‑effective way to scale precision strikes across a broad set of targets.
Versatility across missions and platforms
APKWS has more than a decade of high-volume production behind it with a long record of fielding across U.S. services and partner nations. Designed to transform unguided rockets into precision‑guided munitions, it is combat‑proven for air‑to‑surface, surface‑to‑surface, surface‑to‑air, and air‑to‑air employment.
The kit is qualified on a wide range of platforms, including rotary‑wing and fixed‑wing aircraft, unmanned systems, ground launchers, and maritime vessels. Its rapid integration, easy maintenance, dependable performance, and broad platform compatibility allow units to adopt and deploy the capability quickly in multiple theaters.
That flexibility matters as threats evolve.
In 2025, the U.S. Air Force announced its sprint-like effort to integrate and demonstrate APKWS laser-guided rockets on the F-15E Strike Eagle. The integrated developmental and operational flight testing, including live fire at targets over land and water, was an expedited fielding push to deliver capability to the warfighter immediately. The goal of adding this capability to the Strike Eagle’s arsenal was to bring it into the counter-unmanned aerial system fight in a cost-effective way alongside the F-16.
This year, BAE Systems completed a Eurofighter Typhoon test in the United Kingdom that struck a ground target and set up the next phase of air‑to‑air trials, emphasizing a cost‑effective counter‑UAS option for the Royal Air Force’s (RAF) fighter. Rapid collaboration between industry partners, the RAF, and the Ministry of Defence moved the capability from testing to operational deployment in less than two months. Trials included air‑to‑air engagements that demonstrated effectiveness in real scenarios. APKWS is now in operational use on Typhoon, enhancing versatility and supporting persistent air defense while managing costs and resources more effectively.
In parallel with fighter integrations, the same flexibility is being extended to tactical unmanned platforms.
Recent trials achieved the first air‑to‑air engagement of an APKWS‑guided rocket from a multirotor TRV-150, with zero misses across air‑to‑air and air‑to‑ground shots, demonstrating a low‑cost strike and counter‑UAS option for frontline units. A follow‑on event showcased a three‑shot rocket launcher on the TRV-150, part of an industry‑led effort designed to push precision‑strike capability down to the battalion level.
APKWS was also recently demonstrated on the MQ‑9A Reaper, where flight tests featured multiple types and variations of shot profiles, including aerial targets, all executed flawlessly by MQ‑9A crews using laser‑guided rockets and a specialized launcher.
APKWS also enables surface‑to‑air counter‑UAS from mobile and fixed ground launchers, delivering precise, cost-effective intercepts to bolster base and site defense. Field demonstrations and operational use of ground systems firing APKWS have shown rapid integration and effective engagements, with proximity‑fuzed rockets improving kill probability against small aerial targets. The approach leverages widely available 70‑mm launchers and laser designation to scale capability quickly across units, and it is proven across a variety of platforms to support layered air defense.
Agility, capacity, and speed
BAE Systems continues to scale production to meet demand.
In early 2026, the company delivered the 100,000th APKWS guidance kit, a milestone that reflects sustained demand and a mature industrial base. Production from multiple facilities supports high-volume delivery to U.S. forces and allies while continuous upgrades keep pace with evolving mission needs.
With current production capacity of at least 25,000 kits per year and continuing to expand production, BAE Systems is well‑positioned to meet rising demand.
A recent $1.7 billion, multi‑year IDIQ contract from the U.S. Navy further solidifies this capacity. This production capacity is particularly critical as demand surges for C‑UAS interceptors, with BAE Systems able to deliver tens of thousands of cost‑effective APKWS guidance kits, quickly and reliably.
Together, these milestones underscore an innovative, agile guidance kit at scale, backed by a robust supply chain and established manufacturing capacity.
Counter the threat. Control the cost.
Rising domestic and international demand underscores the value of APKWS as a low‑collateral, cost‑effective counter‑UAS and multi‑mission solution. The guidance kit is available to all U.S. armed forces and to allies via foreign defense sales, providing a reliable, affordable option for precision‑strike effects across platforms.
Built on high‑volume manufacturing and dependable performance, APKWS enables rapid, efficient delivery of advanced capabilities to the warfighter at the scale demanded by today’s operations.

Athletic apparel brand Alo has established a national fulfillment and distribution center in Southaven, Mississippi, investing nearly $176 million and planning more than 400 new jobs . The Mississippi Development Authority announced the project on Oct. 12, after work began in August.
What’s Related
The company is moving into an existing building, where it will occupy up to 1.2 million square feet. Alo also has the option to add returns processing at the facility, although the announcement does not say whether or when that work will begin.
The center will serve customers across the country. Alo plans to fill the new jobs by 2027, according to the state announcement, and company co-president Norm Hullinger said additional hiring is expected during the holiday season .
Mississippi is providing assistance through its Mississippi Flexible Tax Incentive, known as MFLEX. DeSoto County and the city of Southaven are also assisting with the project.
RELATED STORIES: Hitachi Energy Plans $528 Million Mississippi Transformer Plant | Amazon Expands Mississippi Presence with Last-Mile Facility in Saltillo
Shipping orders nationwide
The Southaven operation will handle both fulfillment and distribution for Alo’s apparel business. The announcement identifies it as a national center but does not specify whether it will serve online orders, stores, or both.
Mississippi Development Authority Executive Director PJ Waldrop mentioned transportation access and the local workforce as advantages of the location. The announcement did not provide details about warehouse equipment, automation , shipping volumes or delivery times.
Hiring extends into next year
Alo’s staffing plans include more than 400 new positions, with Hullinger mentioning additional holiday hiring separately. The announcement did not give a number for seasonal positions or provide a breakdown of permanent job roles.
“We’re proud to create more than 400 new jobs upon opening, and many more to come during the holiday season,” Hullinger said.
The state’s timetable places completion of hiring in 2027, even though operations are already underway. Alo’s option to add returns processing could bring another function to the building, but that remains a possible addition rather than an announced operating date.

Fire Storm 250 (Credit: Israel Aerospace Industries)
JERUSALEM — Israel Aerospace Industries has unveiled a trio of new systems at the annual AUSA conference that reflect efforts to adapt existing technologies to emerging battlefield threats.
The new capabilities include a mobile aerostat-based radar as well as a counter-drone interceptor that doesn’t use an explosive warhead. The third system — called Fire Storm 250 and developed with Sig Sauer — is a drone equipped with an M250 machine gun.
Dror Bar, executive vice president at IAI and CEO of the company’s Elta Systems, told Breaking Defense that the new aerostat-radar system, called Point@Air, addresses a shift in how the platforms are being used. Aerostats, which are essentially large balloons or dirigibles, have long been used for surveillance but have become vulnerable to drone attacks due to their static infrastructure, Bar said.
Point@Air combines an aerostat with a phased-array radar that Bar said can detect a wide range of targets, from fighter aircraft and large drones to cruise missiles and maritime targets. At around 70 meters (230 feet) long, the system is designed to operate without fixed infrastructure and can be redeployed to a new location within hours, he said.
The capability addresses a vulnerability Israel recently experienced when Hezbollah targeted a large aerostat in northern Isra el, Bar explained. By al lowing operators to move the aerostat, IAI aims to make it harder for adversaries to pinpoint its position and target it with one-way attack drones.
“When sunset arrives, you just fold it and move to the next hill or two, and when morning comes, your enemy sees that you are not there anymore,” Bar said.
He noted that the system could have applications in homeland security missions, as well as for US Central Command and other military commands.
While its core technology is fully developed, Point@Air remains in the demonstration phase as IAI works with US-based TCOM to adjust the platform’s size and configuration, Bar said. TCOM is the prime contractor for the US Army’s aerostat platforms.
IAI also brought its HawkGuard platform to AUSA as another solution geared toward the rapidly evolving counter-drone sector — which Bar called the “holy grail” for defense companies.
“Everybody is searching for an ultra low-cost effector against drones across the world,” he said.
HawkGuard uses an inert interceptor equipped with a large net rather than an explosive warhead. Radar and optical sensors help guide the interceptor towards its target, forming what Bar described as a closed-loop system.
“This closed-loop system allows you to intercept all kinds of drones in a very cost-effective way without affecting the environment,” he said.
The absence of explosives can make HawkGuard suitable for use in populated environments or near sensitive installations, such as sites containing fuel or other explosive materials. The system “has been widely tested” against a range of threats and is already “deployed with several customers,” Bar said.
Bar said HawkGuard can intercept a range of drones, including those that don’t use communications links. The system combines radar and electro-optical sensors with command-and-control technology to detect, track and guide interceptor drones toward their targets. It’s a relatively short-range syste m, he said, t hough IAI has not publicly disclosed its precise range.
Bar noted that the company sees HawkGuard as an additional layer of defense rather than a standalone solution.
“As we have understood, starting from Ukraine, there is no single silver bullet to kill these drones,” he said. “HawkGuard gives our customers the ability to use a very cost-effective, kinetic, inert effector.” He sees good potential for the system in North America, including to protect US military bases against emerging drone threats.
Sticking with the theme of new systems that combine elements of existing technology, IAI and Sig Sauer also announced the completion of a firing test for Fire Storm 250 — an unspecified tactical UAV equipped with Sig Sauer’s Microlight Remote Controlled Weapon Station (RCWS) and an M250 machine gun. During the test, the drone hovered over a simulated battlefield and fired on targets.
“Firing was conducted from varying distances and altitudes, demonstrating the system’s operational flexibility, integrated safety and accuracy under different conditions,” the companies said in a statement.
The companies declined to disclose which UAV is used for the Fire Storm 250, but images of the system show a drone similar to IAI’s APUS 60. The companies also did not specify how many rounds of ammunition the system can carry.
The company statement noted the drone is a “multi-fuel internal-combustion engine” that can be refueled in the field using commonly available fuel, avoiding lengthy battery-charging cycles or specialized infrastructure.
The companies said the test “demonstrated the system’s ability to combine airborne surveillance, target identification and precision firepower in a realistic battlefield scenario.”
Moshe Levy, executive vice president of IAI and general manager of its Military Aircraft Group, said in the statement that the test demonstrated the potential to integrate weapons with uncrewed aircraft in operational settings. He added that “the next generation of unmanned systems will be defined not only by autonomy, but by how effectively they integrate sensing, decision-making and action within the operational environment.”
Sali Okanin, Sig Sauer’s Israel general manager, added : “We’re proud of the new SIG SAUER M250, which is combat-proven technology. It is a belt-fed platform with greater range than legacy systems and weight savings that not only provide squad-level benefits but also make drone capabilities possible,” Okanin said.

Wisconsin-based We Energies has announced a plan to build a new natural gas-fired power plant at the site of an existing gas-fired facility in the state. The utility earlier this month filed an engineering plan with state regulators for construction of a 750-MW station at the Fox Energy Center, in Wrightstown in the Fox Valley region.
The utility did not reveal an estimated cost for the project, which it calls the Fox North Energy Center. Brendan Conway, a spokesperson for We Energies, in a statement said the new plant will improve power grid reliability and support the growing need for electricity in Wisconsin. “The engineering plan marks the first step in the review process,” Conway said. “Additional information about the project will be provided through regulatory filings in the coming months.”
A recent draft Strategic Energy Assessment from the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin said the state’s peak electricity demand will rise from about 14.2 GW this year and top 20 GW by 2032, a more than 40% increase. The assessment said some 72% of that projected increase is related to three major data center developments planned in the state.
We Energies has not said whether the Wrightstown plant would serve a data center. The new station would be adjacent to the existing 619-MW gas-fired Fox Energy Center, which has operated since 2005. The utility in its proposed timeline for the new plant said construction would not begin until 2029, with the station expected to enter commercial operation in late 2032 if it receives the necessary regulatory approvals.
States across the U.S. have seen numerous proposals to build new natural gas-fired power plants in recent years. A report released earlier this month from Environment America Research & Policy Center and Frontier Group said that data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration shows plans for grid-connected gas-fired power stations have nearly tripled since early 2023, with a nearly 50% increase in the past eight months. The groups said rising demand for electricity from data centers is driving the buildout.
POWER has previously reported on the growing development of natural gas-fired power plants that is in part driven by artificial intelligence and data centers. That includes recent acquisitions of gas-fired facilities by major U.S. power generators such as Vistra and LS Power .
— Darrell Proctor is a senior editor for POWER.

One-Owner 1972 Camaro Hasn't Moved Since Last Millennium, Hides Biggest Small-Block Surprise
51 photos
Photo: YouTube/Not So Fast
The second generation of the Camaro was a roller coaster of extreme proportions, recording both he lowest and the highest production volumes of the that iteration. In 1972, the moniker dropped to an abyssal 68k units, while in 1979 it managed to sell more than 214,000 MORE than in ’72. And this example, coming from that very ill-fated season, sat for almost three decades, patiently waiting for its owner who bought it new to put it back on the road. That wait is over.
1972 was not a good year to be a Camaro. Or a Chevrolet, in general. Or anything General Motors, quite frankly. United Auto Workers had had just about enough of GM’s attitude and walked out of their work stations at the Norwood facility. That was in April. They came back in September.
It doesn’t take a rocket science to see that the strike lasted almost half a year, with the direct consequence being production numbers suffered enormous setbacks. As such, scrupulous gearheads might say that the ‘72s are somewhat… rare ? Maybe not – 68,651 is still a fairly large volume (the Plymouth Barracuda, for example, never managed to hit that mark in its entire decade-long stint), but for the Bowtie pony car, it was a counter-performance of cataclysmic proportions.
So big, in fact, that the brass hats from corporate considered axing the moniker. They eventually ruled in favor of keeping it – thankfully, otherwise the car we see in the video embedded below might have been one of the last Chevrolet Camaros ever made. However, it’s probably among the very few that haven’t seen the light of the third millennium at all, having been shoved in a garage before we started writing the year with a “2” at the beginning.
Photo: YouTube/Not So Fast Picture this. You crack open a dusty garage door and find a 1972 Chevrolet Camaro that has not seen daylight since 1999. It sat there for 27 years just waiting for someone to drag it out. A guy started swapping the intake manifold on a 400 cubic-inch small block V8, got sidetracked, and walked away. The car basically became a shelf until the right wrenchers finally came along.
Those right guys run the Not So Fast YouTube channel. Nathan McInnis and his buddy rolled up with a trailer, strapped the Chevy down, and hauled it back to their shop. You would expect a complete rust bucket after almost three decades, but this Midwest survivor was put only on hold, not on the deathroll. The paint held up well, and engine internals were shockingly clean.
The wrenchers knew better than to just turn the key and pray for luck. They had a method – the right one. The correct approach. The way to do it properly. The true died-in-the-wool piston-head mentality. They started from ground zero, tore out the fuel system. They dropped in a brand-new tank, ran fresh rubber lines, and bolted up a replacement sending unit.
Photo: YouTube/Not So Fast The car’s fluids were drained – block, transmission, rear end, radiator, the pans dropped (engine and cogbox), the differential thoroughly inspected, and then the car received a fresh supply of lubricants and coolant.
Then they yanked the distributor out to manually prime the oil pump. Turning that crank by hand ensured the engine would not chew up its own bearings. Once they saw oil flowing properly, they dumped two-stroke fuel straight down the large carburetor throats.
The old V8 roared to life on the very first try. It smoked out the entire shop, but it ran. Dan yelled, "It is alive!" as the exhaust cleared. They chased down a nasty coolant leak blowing out of a loose thermostat housing. They also discovered a cross threaded brass oil pressure sending unit dumping fluid everywhere. Because old units use actual pressure to read gauges, they fixed it immediately.
Photo: YouTube/Not So Fast Brakes came next, because stopping is somewhat important when one plans to drive their old Camaro after a hefty 27-year pause. In fact, come to think of it, it’s important, no matter what car it may be. They tossed the rusted brake booster and bolted on a fresh master cylinder. They replaced wheel cylinders, ran new hoses, and slapped on some brake pads and rotors.
Throwing on a fresh set of tires, they took the resurrected Chevy around the neighborhood. It clicked through the automatic gears perfectly. "First drive in 27 years. It runs really great!" That pretty much sums it up. If only all classic car resurrections were this successful on the first try…
They took it out on the highway next, cruising smoothly at 60 mph. one of the mechanics rightfully noted no one would never know this thing had been sitting for so long. The boys were having fun with 400 cubes of old-school small-block torque from an age long before they were born. This car is not a factory performance package model, it was born a run-of-the-mill 350, as the fender badges proclaim.
Photo: YouTube/Not So Fast Someone decided a base Camaro deserved better, and threw the biggest-ever Chevy small-block at it (by displacement, not physical sizes). That makes this street brawler the perfect candidate for a budget backyard resurrection.
Seeing a 1972 Camaro back on the road stirs up the history a bit. Back in ‘72, you could walk into a dealership and pick between a few distinct flavors. You had the base model, the split bumper Rally Sport, the Super Sport, or the corner carving Z/28 performance package. The base model, just like our rescue car started out, was the volume leader. Most people bought the standard version because it looked great and did not completely empty out your bank account then.
Let us break down those production numbers . Out of that strike shortened run, buyers opted for 11,364 Rally Sport appearance packages. Another 6,562 customers stepped up to buy the Super Sport version. Only 2,575 buyers shelled out for the hardcore track version. That leaves the vast majority of cars built – 48,139 units – as standard base models. The base coupe started at a very reasonable 2,729 dollars with a six-cylinder engine.
Photo: YouTube/Not So Fast If you wanted V8 power, the base 8-cylinder model sticker price bumped up to 2,819 dollars. Engine options were solid across the entire lineup. The entry level motor was a 250 cubic-inch sixer pushing 110 horsepower. The base V8 was a 307-cuber with 130 horsepower. Next up was the signature 350 cubic-inch V8 (that had debuted hand in hand with the Camaro moniker itself, in the fall of ’66, as a 1967 model) that delivered 165 horsepower for the regular daily street cruiser buyer.
Those wanting even more grunt could grab the Super Sport, which offered a 402 cubic-inch big-block throwing down 240 horsepower, and hidden behind a “396” badge, for marketing purposes. The Z28 offered a high-revving 350 cubic-inch solid-lifter engine pushing 255 horsepower. All numbers are net ratings, because SAE said so.
Chevrolet gave buyers plenty of transmission choices to pair with these engines. You could grab a 3-speed manual, a 4-speed manual, or let the car do the shifting itself. If you wanted an automatic, you got the 2-speed Powerglide on lower models or the heavy-duty 3-speed Turbo Hydra-Matic. Imagine the audacity of carmakers from 50+ years ago when giving windshield wipers the same number of speeds as the car itself…

DHL Global Forwarding has added six dedicated healthcare air routes connecting Europe and North America with pharmaceutical markets in Asia. Announced on Monday , the expansion is for temperature-controlled shipments , including medicines, vaccines and clinical trial materials.
What’s Related
Three routes connect Cincinnati with Singapore, Tokyo Narita and Seoul Incheon. The European routes connect Liège with Shanghai, Brussels with Shanghai, and Brussels with Singapore.
DHL says the routes give pharmaceutical customers more shipping options and greater control over how sensitive cargo is handled. Most flights operate on DHL-branded aircraft, which the company says reduces handovers between transportation providers.
The additions follow the launch of DHL’s Brussels-Cincinnati healthcare route earlier this year.
RELATED: DHL Adds Dedicated Brussels–Cincinnati Cold Chain Route
Protecting cargo in flight and during transfers
DHL uses Boeing 777 freighters with three cargo compartments that can be set to different temperatures. On the ground, thermal blankets and tested handling procedures are designed to limit exposure to temperatures outside a shipment’s required range.
The company’s approach combines controlled transportation with healthcare facilities and packaging selected for each shipment. DHL says it tests shipping routes and packaging against expected conditions, rather than relying on packaging alone to protect cargo throughout the trip.
Its cold chain service also includes shipment monitoring and risk alerts through DHL LifeTrack. These tools let customers track shipments and receive alerts about potential problems during the flight.
When DHL announced the Brussels-Cincinnati service in February, it said the wider operation connected more than 30 aviation hubs and handling locations that follow Good Distribution Practice standards for pharmaceutical shipments. DHL also said its temperature-controlled facilities and transportation could reduce reliance on heavy packaging and refrigerated air freight containers .
Singapore facility is planned for late 2027
The new Singapore routes connect with a separate facility investment announced in September. DHL Global Forwarding plans to open its Singapore Coldchain Hub at Changi Airport in late 2027.
The $22 million facility will cover 3,047 square meters and include handling areas maintained at 2°C to 8°C and 15°C to 25°C. Direct access to the airport’s aircraft operating area is intended to limit temperature exposure as goods move between planes and the facility.
DHL is also adding refrigerated operating and pallet -storage space at its healthcare facility in Indianapolis, about a 2.5-hour drive from its Cincinnati air hub.

U.S. Army Vice Chief of Staff, Gen. Christopher LaNeve, speaks at the 2026 AUSA Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington, D.C., Oct. 12, 2026. (U.S. Army photo by Staff Sgt. Alexander Nieves)
WASHINGTON — The Army’s top officer revealed today that the service has “redesignated” its Futures and Concepts Command (FCC) as the new Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command (FASCOM).
“We are incorporating autonomous and unmanned systems at every single echelon across the formation … with the force structure to match … including introducing UAS [unmanned aerial systems] and robotics military specialties to integrate these technologies at the point of nee d,” Acting Chief of Staff Gen. Christopher LaNeve said at the annual AUSA conference.
“Wi th [Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s] ann ouncement establishing Autonomous Warfare Command , Acting Secretary [Adam] Telle and I have redesignated Futures and Concepts Command to serve as US Army F utures and Autonomous Systems Command … FASCOM,” he said.
Earlier this month the Army announced the establishment of FASCOM along with a handful of other related organizational changes, but at the time did not note FCC’s role. LaNeve didn’t specifically say why Army leaders decided to make the move, but he said it signals that the service is “moving with focus and intention.”
“[As] Acting Secretary Telle likes to say, we are gaining velocity,” he added.
LaNeve sai d in a press re lease prior to his remarks today that FASCOM will be led by a three-star general officer. It will “integrate and ultimately accelerate” the work of the Combat Capabilities Development Command, Medical Research and Development Command, 75th Innovation Command, Joint Modernization Command and the Transformation Decision Analysis Center, he said.
On Sept. 30 D efense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the Pentagon would create a new four-star command , called Autonomous Warfare Command (AUTOWARCOM), centered on drones and similar technology as well as a new working group on the future of defense.
Today’s move makes the FCC a short-lived organization, at least in name. It was activated at the beginning of this year by then-Secretary Dan Driscoll as a subordinate command under the service’s four-star Transformation and Training Command, or T2COM.
T2COM was established as a result of the service’s sprawling Army Transformation Initiative , which aimed to bolster the service’s modernization and consolidate some of the service’s leadership. It combined the service’s two four-star commands, Training and Doctrine Command and Army Futures Command .
“This goes beyond drones,” LaNeve said in the release today. “FASCOM will pioneer operational concepts that harness autonomous capabilities across all warfighting functions.”

This New Destination Trailer Has a Front Kitchen, an Enormous Living Room, and Sleeping for Eight
23 photos
Photo: Recreation by Design
In an RV industry full of choices, most people choose the best-known brands like Thor Industries and Forest River, and smaller independent manufacturers are easy to overlook. However, sometimes it’s worth looking at the underdogs as well, as they often offer better build quality, more innovative layouts, and superior customer service.
Recreation by Design is one of these smaller companies, and today, I’m going to take a look at their new 2027 Baypoint 435 destination trailer, which is designed for families and offers an enormous living room with massive windows, a beautiful kitchen, a master bedroom, and a dual loft.
Based in Elkhart, Indiana, Recreation by Design is a third-generation family business with roots dating back to the 1950s. Unlike the big conglomerates that dominate the market, Recreation by Design doesn’t rely on standardized production. The company builds its own chassis and cabinetry in-house, an approach that allows it to focus on craftsmanship and gives it greater control over some aspects of the finished product, from its structure to the finishes that make an RV feel like home.
The 2027 Baypoint 435 is a new floor plan that has not yet been listed on the manufacturer’s website, so the exact spec list is still a mystery, but Recreation by Design did ship initial production units to dealership lots, and Hunter Megowen from The RV Hunter channel has already filmed a full tour, which you can watch below.
Photo: Recreation by Design As a destination trailer , the Baypoint 435 is not meant to travel frequently. Actually, it’s built for permanent site setup and offers features that make it feel more like a tiny home than an RV. Measuring about 44 feet (13.4 meters) long, this is a dual-axle model with four slide-outs and two entrances. It sits on an in-house-built chassis with heavy-duty I-beams made with certified steel and E-coat corrosion protection.
In terms of construction, the RV features vacuum-bonded laminated sidewalls and hardwood slide surrounds, which contribute to the overall durability, and the slide roofs use laminated fiberglass, which enhances protection against leaks. The company also reinforces the walls around the slide-outs with steel tubing, helping prevent the structures from bowing under their weight over time.
The defining features of the new floor plan are a front kitchen with large windows and a dinette, a beautiful central living area, tall ceilings, and a drop-frame rear bedroom. A large loft with a split design adds another sleeping area, making this destination trailer suitable for families or couples who like to host guests.
Photo: Recreation by Design The kitchen at the front benefits from spectacular views thanks to large windows all around, including a front picture window and an atrium window above the dining area. It is equipped with a full suite of premium GE appliances, ranging from a four-burner range with an oven and a microwave to a residential-style 12V refrigerator with a wine rack above it.
Solid-surface countertops, soft-gray cabinetry, and a ceramic subway-tile backsplash give the space a contemporary appearance . The dining space is located in the front slide-out and consists of a table with a flip-up extension and four chairs. A nice breakfast bar area with two stools is also integrated between the kitchen and living area.
Photo: Recreation by Design The living room is a nice open area with a huge L-shaped sectional sofa, a loveseat across the way, and an entertainment wall with a big TV, electric fireplace, and a sound bar. This setup, combined with tall ceilings and large windows, makes the entire space feel enormous. The sleeper sofa offers an additional bed for guests, and motorized shades on the large windows ensure privacy.
The bathroom is not very big but feels residential with dual stainless-steel sinks, a porcelain foot-flush toilet, a round mirror, storage drawers, and open shelving. The shower is a one-piece fiberglass unit with a seat cutout and four spray ports. Hot water is supplied by an on-demand Fogatti water heater.
Between the drop-frame bedroom, the large loft, and sleeper sofa in the lounge, the Baypoint 435 can accommodate as many as eight people. The master bedroom is designed as a private room with a queen bed and a large closet with cubbies, pull-out compartments, hanging rods, and a compartment with washer/dryer preparation.
Photo: Recreation by Design Above the drop-frame bedroom, the loft can fit two twin mattresses on one side and another double mattress on the other. Protection railings instead of a full wall and a reported headroom of 6 feet 6 inches in the slides maintain a sense of openness.

WARSAW, Poland — Norway’s Kongsberg has decided to build a new production facility for counter-drone systems in northern Poland, with plans to invest more than 200 million zloty ($51 million) in the plant.
The investment is connected to the company’s cooperation with Polish state-run defense group PGZ to deliver the San anti-drone system to the Polish military.
“We have been present in Poland for many years. We think it’s important that we establish local sites in Poland,” Eirik Lie, the president and CEO of Kongsberg, told Defense News at the Warsaw Security Forum here on Oct. 12. “We are on good track for deliveries on the San program. But also, we expect export contracts, so this enables us to be prepared for these exports from Poland.”
Under the San deal, valued at around PLN 15 billion ($3.8 billion), Kongsberg and PGZ are to supply 18 anti-drone batteries, 52 firing platoons, 18 command platoons, and 703 vehicles to the Polish military, according to data from Poland’s Ministry of National Defence. The contract will be largely financed by loans that Poland has secured from the European Union’s Security Action For Europe (SAFE) scheme.
Given the region-wide concern over drone incursions, Lie said Kongsberg expects the demand for its solutions to rise significantly in the coming years. In the future, the envisioned Polish factory could also introduce additional defense solutions to its portfolio.
“As a company, we are expanding quite a lot. We want to build on this factory for other elements as well,” the CEO said.
In a statement, the Norwegian group said it plans to sign a construction contract by the end of 2026 and begin work immediately afterward. Serial production of counter-drone systems could begin in the first half of 2028. The investment is expected to create more than 100 jobs in Poland once the plant reaches full capacity.

The first directed energy weapon selected by the U.S. Army for the Enduring-High Energy Laser (E-HEL) program could be out of testing and ready for counter-drone operations by early 2028, Army officials told Military Times at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington.
“We would love to be able to keep the first unit off the line for our testing and training. However, what we’ve seen is, with the environment as it is, everything that we produce as a capable counter-UAS system tends to get deployed somewhere,” said Kirk Williams, chief engineer at the U.S. Army Directed Energy Project Office.
In September, the Army awarded AeroVironment a $464.8 million contract for LOCUST X3, its modular, palletized high-energy laser system. Earlier generations of the LOCUST system are actively fielded in operational environments, including at the U.S. southern border, according to AeroVironment. The first LOCUST X3 is slated for delivery by Q4 of FY 2027 and will be mounted on the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle.
The goal is to push it through testing, validation, verification and “give it to soldiers as soon as possible,” said Brig. Gen. Guy Yelverton, capability program executive for Defensive Fires. “My far-down point would be spring [2028], and if I could get in the December-January timeframe, that would be awesome. That would be a great win for the Army.”
It is unclear where the first high-energy counter-drone weapons under H-ELS will be deployed. Yelverton suggested the 7th Infantry Division could be a potential partner.
Deputy commanding officer of Support for the 7th Infantry Division, Col. Charles Kean, described directed-energy weapons as a component of defense against high-echelon air threats, including individual UAS or formations, but said they were not a “single bullet” solution.
“The more capabilities we put in the hands of soldiers, the easier they are to maintain, the more reliable they are, the better,” Kean told an audience at AUSA’s Warriors Corner.
The Army successfully demonstrated eight kills using the directed energy platform prototype during the Army Modernization Day in October.
The palletized, modular solutions can be integrated onto a number of vehicles, including the JLTV and Infantry Squad Vehicle, or ISV.
The modular system will improve reliability and sustainability by making it possible for soldiers to perform field-level maintenance, according to Williams. It will also allow the Army to “continuously improve the system over time” without replacing the full unit.
The counter-drone E-HEL contract is for more than 26 laser weapons units total, according to AeroVironment vice president of Directed Energy, John Garrity, who indicated the initial system is on target for 2027 delivery.
“We were able to lean forward with a lot of the long-lead procurements early, so we’re ramping up for production,” Garrity told Military Times. “Because drones aren’t getting any slower and our adversaries aren’t getting any lazier with them.”
Directed energy weapons are one of the capabilities the Army is pursuing at speed to counter the growing threat of low-cost, unmanned aircraft systems.
During an earlier speech at AUSA, Secretary of the Army Adam Telle highlighted the need to field low-cost interceptors to shoot down missiles and drones. Telle hailed the Army’s work to streamline acquisition and get soldiers the gear they need.

U.S. container imports hit a record high in September, up 10.3% from a year earlier to 2.55 million twenty-foot equivalent units, according to Descartes . The company released the findings Oct. 8 in its latest Global Shipping Report.
What’s Related
Imports fell 2.2% from August but were 24.8% above September 2019. Through the first nine months of 2026, total imports were up 0.8% from the same period last year, marking the first time this year that cumulative volume moved ahead of 2025.
Shipments from China were a major part of September’s increase, rising 21.2% from a year earlier. China accounted for 36.3% of all U.S. container imports, compared with 34% in August.
The results also showed a shift toward West Coast ports and longer transit delays at most major ports. Imports from the 10 largest countries of origin were essentially unchanged from August, as gains from China, India, and Taiwan offset declines elsewhere.
China shipments on the rise
U.S. imports from China totaled 924,454 twenty-foot equivalent units, or TEUs, up 4.5% from August. TEUs are a standard measure of container volume based on a 20-foot container.
Plastics led China-origin imports, followed by furniture and bedding, and toys and sporting goods. Those three categories accounted for approximately 38% of September’s container volume from China.
Seven of the top 10 countries supplying U.S. container imports recorded monthly declines. China’s increase largely offset those losses, leaving the group’s overall volume nearly flat.
West Coast ports gain ground
Los Angeles imports rose 8.8% from August, while Long Beach gained 5.9%. Oakland increased 14.4%, and Tacoma rose 7%.
Other major ports recorded declines, including Houston at 16.5%, Norfolk at 13.4%, Charleston at 10.3% and Savannah at 9.6%. Gulf Coast imports overall fell 14.8% to 215,324 TEUs, below their rolling 12-month average.
The five leading West Coast ports handled 46.7% of U.S. container imports in September. The five leading East and Gulf Coast ports handled 39.7% of U.S. container imports in September.
Increased delays at most major ports
Descartes’ transit-delay measure increased at eight of the 10 major ports. New York/New Jersey recorded the largest increase, rising 1.5 days to 8.3 days, while Houston rose 1.4 days to 7.2 days.
The measure compares the initial estimated arrival date on a shipment’s bill of lading with the date Descartes receives the customs-processed shipping record. It should not be read as the number of days a container sits at a terminal.

Source: Rivian
Doug Field, the engineer who ran Tesla’s Model 3 program and later Ford’s entire EV operation, is now president of Mind Robotics, the industrial robotics startup Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe spun out of Rivian last year.
He lands at a company that has now raised more than $1 billion in under a year, and he’ll run product, engineering, and operations alongside Scaringe.
Field’s next job is robots
Field’s résumé reads like a tour of the most ambitious hardware programs in the industry. He was Tesla’s SVP of Engineering through the Model 3 launch, ran Apple’s car effort inside its Special Projects Group, and then spent nearly five years at Ford as chief EV, digital and design officer.
We reported in April that Ford was folding Field’s EV group into manufacturing as he left the company . Ford didn’t replace him with an outside hire, and his department ended up under COO Kumar Galhotra. Five months later, he has his next job.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
In Mind’s announcement, Scaringe called Field “a remarkable leader with a track record of delivering new technologies in successful products,” adding that’s “exactly what Mind needs as we deploy robots into real factories and beyond.”
Field called the combination of AI and robotics “one of the most important—and difficult—engineering challenges of our time.”
A $1 billion war chest and a factory to practice in
Mind Robotics first surfaced as part of Rivian’s Q3 2025 earnings report , with a $115 million seed round led by Eclipse. The money has piled up fast since then:
$115 million seed, led by Eclipse (late 2025)
$500 million Series A, co-led by Accel and Andreessen Horowitz (March 2026)
$400 million round led by Kleiner Perkins (May 2026), which Reuters reported valued Mind at $3.4 billion
That’s roughly $1 billion for a company that hasn’t shown a product publicly. Mind says it’s building foundation models plus “purpose-built” robot hardware for dexterous manufacturing work. It hasn’t said whether any of that hardware is humanoid.
Mind’s real edge is its access. Rivian is a major shareholder and its launch customer, which gives the startup a live, high-volume auto plant to collect training data and deploy robots in. And that plant is busy: the R2 is ramping in Normal, Illinois, and Rivian delivered 19,248 vehicles in Q3 alone.
The Tesla comparison is unavoidable
Field’s hire puts Mind on a direct collision course with the program Tesla now uses to justify much of its valuation: Optimus.
Tesla’s track record there isn’t great. Elon Musk predicted about 10,000 Optimus robots built in 2025, with roughly 1,000 doing useful work in Tesla factories by year-end. In January, he admitted none were doing “useful work.” Tesla then ended Model S and Model X production at Fremont to convert those lines for Optimus, and it has pushed back the Optimus V3 reveal repeatedly . In July, Musk said production would be “extremely slow at first” .
Mind is taking a quieter route. No stage demos, no unit targets. Just robots trained on a real assembly line, with a customer that already owns a stake in the company.
Electrek’s Take
This is a smart hire.
Field is a hardware industrialization guy. That’s his whole career: taking a product that works in a lab and making it work at volume. The Model 3 got to mass production on his watch. It was messy, and he took a leave at the height of “production hell” in 2018 before leaving Tesla, but the car shipped and became the best-selling EV in the world for years.
His record since then is more mixed. The Apple car was canceled after he left. At Ford, Model e lost more than $5 billion in 2024 alone, and the company has since scaled back its EV ambitions. But the low-cost Universal EV Platform and the $30,000 midsize pickup coming out of Louisville in 2027 are his team’s work, and that’s the most promising thing Ford has going in EVs.
So why does Mind need him? Because foundation models are the easy part to fundraise on. Getting robot hardware reliable enough to run shifts in a car plant is where everyone, Tesla included, has struggled.
It also tells us how serious Scaringe is about this. He’s running Rivian through the most important launch in its history, plus Also and now Mind. Bringing in a president with Field’s profile is how you keep Mind from becoming a side project while focusing your needed attention on Rivian.

How much does the 2027 Chevy Blazer EV cost?
Chevy’s electric Blazer is back for the 2027 model year, bringing a few updates and a slightly higher starting price.
The base 2027 Chevy Blazer EV LT starts at $45,000, up $300 from last year’s model. Including the $1,795 destination fee, the starting MSRP comes to $46,795.
The sportier 2027 Blazer EV RS also gets a $300 price hike, and now starts at $52,595. Meanwhile, the range-topping SS trim remains at $62,495.

Upgrading to all-wheel-drive (AWD) adds $3,000 for the LT and RS trims, while the SS comes with standard AWD.
The 2027 Chevy Blazer EV LT and RS use an 85 kWh battery pack, offering up to 312 miles of EPA range in the FWD models. AWD models get 283 miles of range. The range-topping SS uses a larger 102 kWh battery that delivers up to 302 miles of range.

Like all new 2027 GM electric vehicles, the Chevy Blazer EV has a native NACS port so drivers can use Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter.

Samsara has made its Agent Studio platform generally available to all customers, opening its no-code AI agent builder to fleets and other businesses using its software.
Samsara is recording AI-agent interactions about seven times faster than when it launched the tools in June, with its latest 500,000 interactions accumulating in 16 days, down from 112 days initially. Samsara measures AI agent adoption by the number of interactions, which it defines as a complete agent session through chat or voice.
Voice agents surpassed chat in interaction volume within four weeks of launch and have led every week since, Samsara said.
Most voice interactions to date have been calls initiated by agents and configured by the organizations using them, Samsara said. The company said more than 1,000 organizations use Samsara agents weekly, but did not specify how many organizations use voice agents specifically.
Samsara launched Agent Studio in June, but has now made it available to all customers on Tuesday. The platform lets customers build custom AI agents using operational data to perform tasks such as compiling reports, flagging potential hours-of-service violations and answering drivers’ questions based on company policies. The company did not disclose how many customers are using agents in production or how many have built custom agents. Agent Studio is included in existing Samsara subscriptions, the company noted.
The announcement comes as logistics companies work to move AI projects beyond pilot programs and demonstrate financial returns.
A March 2026 Boston Consulting Group survey of more than 180 logistics providers and shippers found that about 40% of logistics service providers had deployed AI beyond pilot programs, but only about 10% had scaled it across core operations. Just 13% reported measurable value from AI. Unclear returns on investment and gaps in internal capabilities were among the leading barriers to broader adoption.
A separate September 2026 survey by Descartes found that 19% of shippers and 15% of logistics service providers were using AI at scale. The findings suggest that while AI is gaining a foothold in transportation, many companies have yet to deploy it broadly across their operations.
“AI is quickly adopted when it’s useful, and in physical operations that means an agent has to understand the operation and meet people where the work happens,” said Johan Land, Samsara’s chief product officer.
Samsara cited several customers using agents for reporting, compliance monitoring and driver communication.
Grand Isle Shipyard uses an agent to compile forms, inspection reports and asset data into monthly reports. Samsara said the process takes about five minutes per division, cutting report-generation time by 99%. The company estimated the change frees up about $100,000 in annual specialist capacity, though it did not provide the calculation behind that figure.
S. Bertram Foods uses an agent to track remaining stops, driving time and shift time to flag potential hours-of-service violations three hours in advance. Samsara said the system reduced weekly manual review time by 84%.
StreamTech Industrial uses an agent to identify trips in which drivers have not logged into their vehicles. Samsara reported a reduction of 500 hours in unassigned driving over two months.
The customer results were supplied by Samsara, which did not provide detailed measurement methods for all the reported outcomes.
Voice agents bring AI into the cab
Samsara says its voice agents can call drivers with instructions when trucks arrive at unfamiliar facilities, including information about entrances, parking, yard speed limits and required safety equipment. Drivers can ask follow-up questions, while managers can use operational data to investigate issues such as extended facility stops.
Specifically, Samsara said its voice agents deploy through its dash cams and operate hands-free. The hands-free design is significant because federal rules prohibit commercial drivers from holding a phone while driving, while allowing hands-free phone use. Organizations can configure agents to activate under specified conditions, such as when a vehicle enters or exits a designated geofence.
The company also offers Samsara Assistant , which lets users query operational information through its software dashboard, and Samsara MCP, which connects authorized Samsara data to external AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude and Microsoft Copilot. Agent Studio adds a way for customers to create custom chat and voice agents for their own workflows.
For freight and logistics operators, the potential benefit is less time spent gathering information, monitoring compliance and answering routine questions. But the announcement offers limited evidence of how widely the agents are being deployed or whether the reported time savings translate into sustained financial returns. Those questions will matter as logistics companies weigh further investment in AI.
Why this matters:
Freight and logistics companies are looking for ways to turn AI pilots into tools that deliver measurable operational value. Samsara’s usage figures suggest growing engagement with AI agents, but the company has not disclosed how many customers have deployed them or provided detailed methods behind customer-reported efficiency gains. Those metrics will help determine whether AI agents can deliver sustained returns beyond early use cases.

FIA Prez Ben Sulayem Claims F1 Cars Will Go V8 Next Decade
8 photos
Photo: Max Verstappen on Facebook
Formula 1 will race with V8 power units again from the 2030 season, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem announced today in the capital of Rwanda, on a stage built for the launch of the African Grand Prix. Regarding the latter announcement, a 10-year agreement returns the sport to the African continent for the first time since the 1993 edition of the South African Grand Prix.
On a panel with Formula 1 chief exec Stefano Domenicali and Rwandan prez Paul Kagame, the big kahuna at the Federation Internationale de l'Automobile said that Rwanda will hear the new V8s in the early 2030s. Putting an emphasis on 2030s because it's not clear if the Bugesera circuit near Kigali will be ready in 2030.
Sulayem kept its V8 confirmation relatively short, giving it a 2030 launch date and a venue where it will race in the 2030s. There is, however, no rulebook to speak of as of this writing. A vote on the V8 era hasn't been held either, and don't even dare ask about specifications every manufacturer has to abide by.
For the time being, it's generally agreed that a displacement of 3.0 liters is on the menu. There is also talk about a turbocharger and a much smaller electric side of the powertrain. If these details prove on point, look forward to a vastly different V8 era from the 2.4-liter naturally aspirated recipe from 2006.
A naturally aspirated V8 would blow past the noise limits of several current Formula 1 venues, with street circuits being the biggest problem for the new eighter. Given the aforementioned, a turbocharger would help the 3.0-liter mill absorb part of the sound as the turbine sits in the exhaust flow.
Photo: Max Verstappen on Facebook Electrification, meanwhile, has been unpopular with the manufacturers and fans alike. From 2030 onward, electrification could survive with a 100-kW boost rather than a 50:50 split for today's V6 turbo power units. At the end of the day, however, nothing past V8 and 2030 has been confirmed by Sulayem to date.
Given that the current regulation cycle should run through the end of 2030 , teams are extremely likely to be asked if they're fine with ending the 50:50 turbo V6 hybrid era in 2029. Speaking from the standpoint of a motorsport lover with some rallying experience to his name, the FIA president said that going V8 would make the next generation of cars approximately 80 kilograms (176 pounds) lighter.
A different objective of the new era is 50 percent less research and development on the powertrain side, which is a tremendous improvement from the current V6 power units. Speaking of, Ben Sulayem made a clear distinction between the sounds F1 enthusiasts want and the boring noises they do not. Sustainable fuels are yet another piece of the puzzle, though it's not clear what kind of green fuels are planned for the new eighter.
Standardization is certain to play a big role in the new era, and there's also talk about a push-to-pass mode. A potential issue with the V8 era is that certain teams won't be happy about ditching the V6 so quickly after entering the sport. Those outfits are, of course, Cadillac and Audi.
