Ridden: 2026 Aprilia RS 660 Made Me Feel Younger for a Day
56 photos
Photo: autoevolution
I live near a city where motorcycles are quite popular, with more and more of them showing up on public roads each year. It’s quite a big hub for the phenomenon, with one event bringing in thousands of riders to celebrate their love for bikes of all shapes and sizes.
I’ve noticed an interesting phenomenon: every high school in town has at least five or six motorcycles parked outside. It’s usually a line-up of Yamaha R125s and Honda CBR125s, but these days CFMoto models have become a popular option due to their affordability.
I’m going to sound old here for a moment, but “back in my day” there was only one highly-desirable option out there: the Aprilia RS 125. I’m obviously talking from the perspective of someone who only cared about riding bikes on public roads and not through forests. I think I must have been roughly 12 when I realized how much I wanted an RS 125.
Back then, it was an aspirational machine, as the RS 50 and Yamaha TZR50 were slightly more accessible, and some people thought they could avoid getting a motorcycle license by choosing this option. Spoiler alert: they couldn’t. Anyway, I haven’t seen an RS 125 on public roads in ages, and it pains me to say that.
In trying to deal with the downsides of a 2-stroke engine, the switch to a 4-stroke setup may have robbed it of its magic. But the world has changed over the past 20 years, and companies that want to survive in the new environment have no choice but to adapt.
Photo: Florin Profir for autoevolution I’ve seen what my nephew is like: he thinks my RX-7 is cool but can’t stand dealing with the smell of oil and gasoline, the noise and the driving particularities of it all. I’m not even saying he’s wrong, as I realize I might just be too nostalgic to observe the progress. But I have to say that even after I’ve ridden dozens of fast motorcycles over the past eight years, I still want an RS 125 in my garage.
And that should explain why I’ve been curious about Aprilia’s RS660 from the moment I saw it at the 2019 EICMA show. By that point in my life, I had realized the RS125 just wouldn’t satisfy my “need for speed”. And all I could think about was spending a few years in the saddle of my Suzuki SV650S before moving on to either an Aprilia RSV Mille or an RSV4. Being a novice rider, all I could think about was that sort of progression.
But I’ve since learned having a liter bike on the road might just be too much, especially if you plan on sticking to the speed limit. You live and you learn, you grow old and you (technically) grow wiser. And while part of me is still screaming “get an early 2000s 600cc machine”, the “wise” part realizes that’s still too extreme for road-use/commuting. So maybe all these new middle-weight sport bikes we can opt for now are on on to something.
I decided I’ve waited too long for a shot at riding the RS660 , and phoned up the people at The Bike Hub in Bucharest, Romania to ask if I could borrow one for the day. They were happy to help out, and I’ve walked in enough motorcycle dealerships to know these guys are truly passionate about bikes. To me, that’s a crucial factor in deciding where to buy my next ride from.
Design Evaluation Photo: Florin Profir for autoevolution People will often tell you that if you don’t look back at your car after you’ve parked it, you’ve bought the wrong car. I still get “I can’t believe I’m driving this after so many years of wanting one” every single time I’m in my RX-8, and it’s even more intense when I switch into the FC.
There are only a few things I miss about living in the big city: being able to order pizza or Chinese food, going karting with my friends, and what some would call “speedhunting”. I often enjoy walking through a neighborhood just to see what bikes or cool cars I can spot.
And I’ll stop, stare and take photos of one as often as I can. What I’m trying to say here is that the RS660 is the kind of machine that will have that same effect on me.
I could almost feel my knees shaking when I first saw it in the showroom, but I couldn’t fully appreciate it until it was out front and not surrounded by all the other bikes and scooters inside.
Photo: Florin Profir for autoevolution To me, the only other machine in this class that comes close to looking as exciting is the Yamaha R7. It really does feel like a baby RSV4, and I’m sure you’ll agree my Alpinestars leathers and Ruroc AT4.0 Cobra Track helmet (which I’ve become fond of) are a much better match for the Aprilia than they were for the BMW F900 GSA .
I’m somewhat disappointed you can’t order a new RS660 in Acid Yellow anymore, but the new Venom Yellow/black finish (with the red wheels) is growing on me as it feels more in tone with Aprilia’s legacy.
You can still opt for Blue Marlin or the slightly more extreme Shakedown Yellow if you don’t mind spending a bit more for the Factory version of the bike. The front winglets will make you feel like a MotoGP rider for the day (which is great considering now has three riders in the Top 4 rankings, with Jorge Martin leading the way on his RS-GP26).
Every single angle of the RS660 is exactly what you’d dream of for a motorcycle in its class, and I must’ve looked at the photos my colleague took over 100 times now. The only element I can’t fully wrap my head around is how short the tail is, and I can just hear my wife blatantly refusing to ride pillion.
Riding Take Photo: Florin Profir for autoevolution I want to make it clear from the get-go that this is by no means a definitive review of the RS660, as there’s only so much ground you can cover in five or six hours riding through a busy city. And it’s obvious I could only explore half of the RS660’s story, as it deserves a few laps at the racetrack (or at least some twisties) to show its true potential. I will tell you this: it made me feel younger for a day.
It put a huge smile on my face that I couldn’t shake for days, and I know it had to be just an appetizer for the time being. If I were to decide on buying a brand-new motorcycle, it would definitely be on the short list.
Also, I might ask for a longer session next so we can come up with a more detailed video and story on what it’s like. I doubt it will happen this year, as temperatures in my area have already plummeted, but I’ll think about it for 2027.
I picked the bike up in a busy part of town, and I guess my knees weren’t just shaking because of how pretty it looked like. I had ridden the Honda CBR650R at the racetrack back in 2023, and let’s just say I hadn’t thought about it since.
Photo: Florin Profir for autoevolution The moment I swung my leg over the RS660 was heartwarming to say the least. It had taken me 20 years to finally ride an Aprilia sports bike, and I knew it would be considerably more thrilling than the old RS125 I used to dream about during my teenage years.
I was slightly concerned that the 659 cc parallel-twin engine would be disappointing, as I’m still stuck thinking a V-configuration would have been the better choice. Let’s not forget that the RS660’s engine is derived from its big bro’s V4, and with the 270 degree crankshaft design you could fool anyone into thinking it’s a V2 setup. Seeing is believing, and what happened next is the reason why I advise anyone to go out for a test ride before making a purchase.
All my concerns were blown away the moment I had a clear path in front of me. I rode away in “Commute”, and didn’t even switch to the Dynamic for the first 30 minutes. Once you hit 4,000 rpm you start to understand why the RS660 is such a popular choice these days, even though peak torque (52 lb-ft/71 NM) comes in at 8,400 rpm. You’ll have to go even higher than that for peak power (105 hp), and I guess that’s one excuse to rev it up to 10,400 rpm.
I realize different people will have a different experience riding any motorcycle, but I can say giving it the full twist of the wrist wasn’t terrifying (which is probably one of the ways you can define this category of bikes).
Photo: Florin Profir for autoevolution It also didn’t feel underwhelming like it did on the CBR650R. The throttle response is slightly better in Dynamic, and I almost couldn’t shake the feeling that the whole bike felt more eager to break the speed limit.
And while the Traction Control, Wheelie Control and Engine Braking characteristics change when using this riding mode, there’s no intervention for the Kayaba suspension front or rear. On the road, I didn’t even feel the need for an adjustment like that, and I imagine going for the Factory version of the motorcycle is the way to go if you intend to spend most of the time at the track.
That’s because it comes standard with Ohlins parts front and rear, which should explain the $2,300 price difference (according to data available for the US market). To me, the RS660 felt extremely compliant, flickable and nimble all at once, and its wet weight of only 183 kg is just one part of the equation. Both variations of the model use the same double 320 mm floating disc with Brembo radial calipers up front, and a 220 mm disc with Brembo calipers in the rear.
Modulating the latter while squeezing through traffic at low speeds felt like second nature, with the front brake always rising to the occasion every time I required it to. Again, it was all a sensible test, and the RS660 aced every road-going challenge. It was enough for me to recommend it to my buddy Omar, who is currently looking for a new motorcycle as he’s had enough dealing with the gremlins on a 25+ year old bike ( my old SV650S ).
Everyday Living Photo: Florin Profir for autoevolution When I picked up the RS660, it had roughly half a tank of gas left in it with an estimated range of almost 100 miles (161 km). The tank’s capacity is 4 gallons (15 liters) and chances are you could ride it for almost 200 miles (321 km) if you behave.
You probably won’t be able to play nice, though, as it’s just too fun to keep going through the gear, especially since it has an up/down quickshifter as standard.
I’m not quite used to a modern setup like this having ridden mostly older bikes, and I found myself using the clutch on multiple occasions at least in the first part of the day.
I’m also not experienced enough to do away with all the rider aids, which is strange considering my previous phrase. I didn’t have any rider aids before and I was fine that way, but there’s some peace of mind that comes “packaged” with that sort of tech.
Photo: Florin Profir for autoevolution The RS660 makes for a spirited commute, with an accent on spirited. There’s still some comfort to enjoy there, and the proof for that lies in the fact that I didn’t have to deal with any wrist or lower back pain after several hours of riding.
But you can see that it wants to go fast, and I’d say it’s a shame if you bought one and never tracked it. The “base” RS660 starts at $11,849 in the US, while the Factory version takes it up a notch to $14,149. I’m not saying the standard exhaust isn’t enough, but I also think a bike like this needs the SC Project system to really score a 5 out of 5.
I would also go for the TPMS and maybe even the carbon belly pan, and those two alone could add about $1,000 in extra cost. So yes, the RS660 is more expensive than the CBR650R, the Daytona 660, the R7 and the GSX8R.
I haven’t ridden the latter three, but after hours of watching and reading countless reviews online, I’m sure my money would go to Italy. I’ll make it a priority to test them all in 2027 for a more accurate conclusion.
Conclusion Photo: Florin Profir for autoevolution Speaking of which, the only reason I’m not rating this bike a 5 out of 5 isn’t because it didn’t have the SC Project exhaust. It’s because I didn’t get to ride it away from traffic, on the track or one of my local mountain roads.
I have no doubt I’d be the limiting factor there, but I’m aiming to become a better rider with each passing year. I’ve looked at every single motorcycle manufacturer on the market, and I can honestly say that I would immediately opt for the Aprilia RS660 if part of me didn’t still think about exploring the continent on an F900 GSA.
That’s an internal battle I have to deal with, although I realize the only satisfying decision would be to get them both. That said, I think the RS660 works great if you’re still in your early years of riding (ideally if you’ve already racked up some miles on something with less power) but also when you’ve already been in the saddle for a while.
It has been my desktop wallpaper for several days now, and I know we must meet again sometime soon.
Rating: 4.5/5 Pros Exciting, MotoGP inspired looks that make every other bike in this category look boring or silly by comparison (except for the Yamaha R7). I’ll list this in the “Cons” section too, just because I needed to fill in the blanks, but the engine and exhaust combo are thrilling to listen to and use even in stock form It strikes the right balance between sportiness and comfort, without being too harsh on your wrists and lower back or shying away its racing DNA.
Cons not really the bike’s fault, but it does feel a bit crammed if you’re 6 feet tall (183 cm) and weigh over 210 pounds (95kg). nostalgia speaking here again but I wish we could go back to a mix of an analog tachometer and a smaller, complementary digital dash my third concern has to do with the standard exhaust system. It’s too tame for my taste, but there’s an easy fix as Aprilia offers an optional, road-legal, SC Project exhaust system for roughly 2,184 Euro/ $2,443 (Romanian market price)

Key takeaways
U.S. gross federal debt passed $40 trillion in August 2026; about $32.4 trillion of it is held by the public.
Net interest on the debt now runs above $1 trillion a year and eats roughly 18.5% of federal revenue, a record.
Heavy Treasury borrowing competes with private borrowers for capital (“crowding out”), adding upward pressure on interest rates, though the near-term rate story is still mostly inflation and the Fed.
Freight feels it first: truck loans start around 7.9% to 8.9%, Class 8 orders are down year over year, small carriers are under strain, and warehouse development costs more to finance.
Anyone planning a fleet replacement cycle or a long-term warehouse lease should model both Fed policy and the structural deficit.
On last week’s Freightonomics show, we discussed CBO rule-of-thumb numbers on how much an increase in the interest rate (as shown by the Effective Federal Funds Rate) would impact the debt. I had in my mind publicly held debt when I said it was somewhere in the neighborhood of $34T. Turns out I transposed a couple numbers and was thinking 34.2 (getting old stinks). It’s actually $32.4T, which is still not good. I looked this morning to see what the total U.S. debt total currently is. That number is worse yet.
Source: usdebtclock.org , 09/23/2026
Gross federal debt crossed $40 trillion in mid-August 2026, months earlier than most forecasters had penciled in, as the Washington Post reported at the time, and it has held in that neighborhood since, touching $40.12 trillion in Treasury’s own daily debt-to-the-penny data as of September 21. Of that total, $32.4 trillion is debt held by the public and $7.7 trillion is intragovernmental, per Congress’ Joint Economic Committee Debt Dashboard . Debt held by the public alone is now running close to 100% of GDP (Debt Clock’s 122.75% is gross federal debt, public plus intragovernmental), and the Congressional Budget Office projects that ratio to reach 120% by 2036 and 175% within thirty years, surpassing the 1946 postwar record of 106% along the way. The debt has roughly doubled in under a decade.
Before we go further, we need to talk about scale. “Trillion” looks fine on paper, but it is difficult to wrap our heads around just how big that number is. To be perfectly honest, one almost needs a metaphor to understand the metaphor, but I’m going to try my best. I don’t want to bore you with too many conversions, but we need to establish some foundations for this. Let’s assume that each dollar of federal debt is one drop of water, 1/20th of a milliliter, or 1/100th of a teaspoon. On my kid’s medicine syringe, 1 tsp = 5 ml; so that math checks out. Following our earlier assumption, that means each teaspoon is a $100 bill of debt. According to World Aquatics , a long-run Olympic-sized swimming pool is 50m x 25m x 2.5m or about 164’1” x 82’ x 8’2”. This means it holds 3,125,000 liters of water, or 825,538 gallons. That means each pool holds 62.5 billion drops. For a federal debt of $40.1T, that means almost 642 pools. Imagine trying to swim that, much less drink that much. If you drank a gallon of water a day, it would take you 2,260 years to down all that. (See what I meant about the metaphor needing a metaphor?)
For freight and logistics, the headline number is not the worrying thing by itself. It’s what a debt stock this large, growing this fast, does to the price of capital, and freight is one of the most capital-intensive, most interest-rate-sensitive sectors in the economy.
Interest on the national debt now tops $1 trillion a year
One small bit of good news is that neither we nor the federal government need to drink that much pool water, at least not all at once. Federal debt gets bought and sold, comes due and gets reissued, on a constant basis. One credit card gets paid off, another gets issued. But, the feds have to pay interest on the money they borrow, just like everyone else. This cost is called “servicing” the debt. And, since the feds both borrow debt and gain interest on balances held (just like in your savings account), the reported numbers are the net of the two.
Net interest on the debt ran $1.02 trillion for the first eleven months of FY26, up 9% from $933 billion over the same span in FY25, and annualized interest costs crossed the $1 trillion mark in August, according to the Peterson Foundation’s interest tracker . Interest is now the second-largest line in the federal budget after Social Security, ahead of defense and Medicare individually and, on a 2025 full-year basis, ahead of the entire defense budget outright, Fortune reported this month. Interest payments now consume roughly 18.5% of federal revenue, above the prior record of 18.4% set in 1991, and CBO projects that share to reach 25% by 2036, with cumulative net interest over the next decade totaling $16.2 trillion. None of that money buys roads, ports, or anything else freight moves for. It is a pure transfer to whoever holds the debt.
How federal debt raises the cost of capital
The 10-year Treasury yield sits at 4.97% as of this week, near a 19-year high, with hawkish Fed commentary on further rate hikes doing a good part of the near-term work, per Trading Economics’ yield tracker . That’s a useful caveat before reaching for the debt as the sole explanation: a meaningful share of the current move is monetary policy responding to inflation, not fiscal policy responding to the deficit. It’s also worth noting the 30-year yield, at roughly 5%, is ordinary by the standards of the last fifty years: it was around 8% in 1991 and over 10% before that, the same Fortune piece notes. Rates this high aren’t historically unprecedented, even if they’re a shock relative to the 2010s.
That said, the deficit is doing its own work on the margin . FY26’s deficit is running around $1.9 to $2 trillion, or 5.8% of GDP, a level CBO itself flags as historically unusual with unemployment below 5%, a point the Peterson Foundation has made as well. That’s the textbook crowding-out setup: the Treasury needs buyers for an ever-larger volume of new debt, and it has to compete for the same pool of savings that would otherwise fund corporate bonds, mortgages, and equipment loans. As economist Ed Yardeni told Fortune , capital flowing into corporate bonds is capital not flowing into Treasuries, and Treasury yields have had to rise to clear the market. Treasury has also doubled its buyback operation size to $4 billion per transaction, a form of direct market management that analysts have described as blurring the line between routine cash management and yield control, which is itself a signal that debt absorption is not frictionless right now.
The academic version of this is the Penn Wharton Budget Model’s capital crowd-out estimates: in a partially open economy where foreign investors finance about 40% of new issuance, each additional trillion dollars of non-productive borrowing is estimated to reduce the private capital stock by roughly 0.65% to 0.78% by mid-century and GDP by 0.23% to 0.28%. Scale that to the trillions being added annually now, and the effect compounds, though it is partly cushioned as long as foreign capital keeps showing up to buy Treasuries.
Where higher interest rates show up in freight and trucking
Equipment financing. Trucking runs on borrowed capital for its rolling stock, and commercial truck loan rates are currently starting around 7.90% to 8.90% for well-qualified borrowers, per LendingTree’s lender survey . That rate environment is a direct pass-through of the Treasury curve plus a lender’s margin. It shows up in the order books: preliminary Class 8 net orders for August 2026 came in around 13,000 to 13,200 units, down 14% to 19% year over year, the eighth straight year-over-year decline, and well below the ten-year average of roughly 23,100 units, Commercial Carrier Journal reported. FTR’s Dan Moyer points to fleets extending truck lifespans and absorbing higher maintenance costs rather than replacing equipment, with high interest rates cited as one factor among several, alongside tariff uncertainty and the 2027 EPA NOx standard. Financing cost isn’t the only story here, but it’s a real one.
Small-carrier attrition. More than twenty trucking and logistics firms filed for bankruptcy in May 2026 alone, FreightWaves reported. The primary drivers FreightWaves points to are erratic demand and elevated operating costs, fuel chief among them, plus margins that stay thin even when spot rates rise, rather than financing costs specifically. But for the segment of the industry running on leased or financed equipment, a higher cost of debt is a background pressure that compounds every other stress carriers are already under, even where it isn’t the headline cause.
Warehouse and DC development. Industrial building loan rates were around 6.58% as of June 2026, per SelectCommercial , and industrial bridge loans are running 7.5% to 9.5% this year, according to PeerSense . That raises the hurdle rate for new distribution center development at exactly the moment e-commerce and nearshoring are pushing demand for well-located industrial space. Slower new supply growth is a second-order effect worth watching for anyone modeling warehouse rents and network footprints over the next few years.
Current market backdrop. For context, SONAR’s national snapshot as of September 22 shows tender rejections (STRI) at 14.21, up about 1% week over week and up 5.6% over the past month; spot rates at $3.43 per mile, up 48.7% year over year; and contract rates at $2.66 per mile, up 15.7% year over year. Diesel, meanwhile, is at a record national average of $6.53 per gallon, but that’s mostly a geopolitical story (the Iran conflict, Russian refinery strikes, a Russian export ban, and historically low inventories), not a debt story, as Logistics Management’s coverage of the EIA data makes clear. It’s worth keeping that distinction clean: rising rates are being driven by a mix of tight capacity, fuel cost pass-through, and the financing backdrop described above, and it would be a mistake to attribute all of it to Washington’s borrowing.
SONAR Ticker: STRI.USA
The honest takeaway for carriers, shippers and brokers
The crowding-out case for freight isn’t that the debt is single-handedly setting truck loan rates or capping warehouse construction. It’s that a structurally larger, faster-growing debt load adds a persistent upward bias to the cost of capital across the economy, and freight, as one of the most financing-dependent, thin-margin sectors there is, feels that bias earlier and more acutely than most. The near-term rate story is still mostly about inflation and the Fed. The multi-decade story, with interest costs on a path to a quarter of federal revenue and debt-to-GDP heading well past the postwar record, is increasingly about the deficit itself. Anyone underwriting a fleet replacement cycle or a ten-year warehouse lease should be modeling both.
Frequently asked questions
How big is the U.S. national debt in 2026?
Gross federal debt passed $40 trillion in mid-August 2026 and stood at about $40.12 trillion on September 21, per Treasury’s Debt to the Penny data. About $32.4 trillion is debt held by the public and $7.7 trillion is intragovernmental.
How much does the federal government pay in interest on the debt?
Net interest ran $1.02 trillion in the first eleven months of FY26, up 9% from the same span in FY25, and annualized interest costs crossed $1 trillion in August. Interest now takes about 18.5% of federal revenue, and CBO projects that share to reach 25% by 2036.
What is crowding out, and how does it affect freight?
Crowding out happens when heavy government borrowing competes with private borrowers for the same pool of savings, pushing interest rates higher. Freight is one of the most capital-intensive, rate-sensitive sectors, so higher borrowing costs show up quickly in truck financing, equipment orders, carrier margins, and warehouse development.
Is the national debt the reason freight rates are rising?
Not primarily. As of September 22, SONAR data shows tender rejections (STRI) at 14.21 and spot rates up 48.7% year over year, driven by tight capacity, record diesel prices, and the financing backdrop. The debt acts as a persistent background pressure on the cost of capital rather than the direct cause of today’s rate moves.

The Port of Los Angeles moved 1.42 million TEUs in September, its best single month ever and the highest monthly volume ever recorded by a port in the Western Hemisphere, Executive Director Gene Seroka said this week. He said lower tariff levels, resilient consumer demand, and cargo shifting away from constrained Panama Canal and Suez routes drove the surge.
Record quarter
September imports totaled 546,000 loaded TEUs, up 19% year over year and 26% above the port’s five-year average. Exports rose 10% to 126,000 loaded TEUs, while the port handled a record 371,000 empty containers as carriers repositioned equipment to Asia.
July through September was the port’s strongest quarter on record at nearly 3 million TEUs, and June through September moved nearly 4 million containers. Through September, 2026 volume stood at nearly 8.1 million TEUs, up about 3% from the same period in 2025.
Seroka said the port expects October volume of about 900,000 TEUs. He cited typhoon-related schedule disruptions in Asia, cargo “roll pools” before China’s national holiday, and continued holiday-season replenishment as reasons volumes should remain elevated.
Trade and sourcing shifts
Seroka in a media briefing said Vietnam is now the port’s second-largest trading partner behind China, while Thailand has entered the port’s top five for the first time. Vietnam-origin volume through Los Angeles has quadrupled over the past decade, he said.
He said China’s share of port business has fallen from 60% to 40%, but added that diversification has been slower than many importers would like. Harvard Business School Professor Willy Shih, the briefing’s guest, said companies are increasingly “optimizing for options” rather than lowest cost, because frequent policy changes make long-term commitments difficult.
Shih said apparent shifts away from China often reflect changes in final assembly rather than a true reduction in upstream dependence, since Vietnam and Mexico still rely heavily on Chinese components. Building comparable supplier networks in Mexico could take about a decade, he said.
Tariffs and outlook
Seroka said tariffs remain a central source of uncertainty, with importers making rapid decisions based on cost, demand, and policy deadlines. He said purchase orders in Asia remain solid, but November and December are difficult to forecast.
He also said ocean carriers and shippers are shifting more cargo to Los Angeles from Panama Canal routings because of drought-related constraints and higher fuel costs tied to Middle East conflict. Shorter, faster transits have become more valuable, he said.
On operations, Seroka said the port is generally flowing smoothly, with truck turns healthy and large vessels turning in about four days. But he flagged rail dwell times as an area requiring close monitoring as the port moves holiday cargo inland.

Last year, Washington, D.C.-based Rivet was one of two contractors selected for the U.S. Army’s Soldier Borne Mission Command program, an effort to develop a device that enhances situational awareness and communication on the battlefield.
Since then, Rivet has raised $55 million in Series A financing and delivered its first 70 prototypes to the Army, according to co-founder and chief executive Dave Marra.
While the other contractor, Anduril, developed a headset resembling the original Integrated Visual Augmentation System, or IVAS, which it had also helped develop, Rivet took a different approach: a pair of militarized smart glasses called the Rivet Hard Spec.
Marra explained in an interview with Military Times that the idea behind the Hard Spec is helping people who “do hard jobs in hard places.”
While the initial goal was to give infantrymen actionable information for targeting and navigation, the application has expanded to other tasks, including technical and mechanical work that soldiers may not perform regularly.
He explained that the idea isn’t to turn an infantryman into an IT specialist or mechanic, but rather, the glasses could give a trained professional the correct procedures for a task without requiring a physical manual.
“So it’s not just like, ‘Hey, we want to create one solution for every military occupational specialty,’” Marra said. “[It’s] what you want to do as a multifunctional soldier or Marine or airman. And this kind of technology is a great accelerator to exactly that.”
He added that Rivet is also adapting the technology for other fields , primarily aerospace manufacturing and aircraft and motor pool maintenance.
“If you happen to forget or you’re not 100% proficient in this role or you don’t do this particular procedure every single day, you can very easily see how a step could be overlooked, especially when you’re in a high-stress environment,” he said.
The startup Rivet Rivet was one of two contractors selected for the U.S. Army’s Soldier Borne Mission Command program, an effort to develop a device that enhances situational awareness and communication on the battlefield. (Rivet)
The company’s longer-term goal is even more ambitious: enabling soldiers to use the glasses to command AI agents that can control robots and drones on the battlefield.
Marra said that means moving beyond using AI to provide a reasoned response to a complicated question.
“I’m asking an agent to go do something on my behalf,” he said. “What we want to get is where an agent and a robot can task each other.”
He said soldiers should be able to communicate with those systems “in common language, not command language.”
For example, he said, a soldier could tell a drone: “‘Hey, there is a target over that hill. Please orbit over that hill and reconnoiter it and send me back the video.’”
If that sounds familiar, it’s because the concept is almost identical to the MacGuffin in the 2019 film Spider-Man: Far From Home . In the movie, Spider-Man and the villain Mysterio fight over a pair of glasses that connect the wearer to an AI-enabled global defense system.
“And the best way to do that today is having a pair of glasses that has eyes and ears on [the AI],” Marra said. “So in many cases, I would say that we’re putting eyes and ears on AI, and then allowing this kind of agentic ensemble to happen within the human workforce.”

TrusTrace released a new report finding that 21% of surveyed fashion brands selling into the United States have had a shipment detained by U.S. Customs and Border Protection . The report also found that 75% are not fully prepared to prove where their materials came from when asked.
What’s Related
The report, The Enforcement Era: Fashion’s Compliance Readiness in Numbers , examines how brands collect supplier information, monitor compliance , and prepare documentation. TrusTrace launched it at the Textile Exchange Conference in Vancouver.
The report found a sharp drop in trusted supplier information beyond the factories making finished products. While 75% of surveyed brands reported trusted data at that first supplier level, only 20% had it at the raw material and farm level.
Where brands are missing supplier information
Other findings show where respondents face gaps:
Shipment detention risk : Among U.S.-selling brands that had not experienced a detention, 58% considered it a realistic near-term risk.
Upstream supplier information: Trusted data fell to 33% at Tier 3, which covers yarn and fiber, before dropping further at the raw material level.
Supplier screening : Nearly half (48%) of U.S.-selling respondents had not screened suppliers against U.S. government forced labor entity lists.
Compliance monitoring: Only 21% reported continuous, automated compliance checks across suppliers, while 17% still relied on spreadsheets and email.
Digital product passports: Although 69% were actively preparing for digital product passports, that group rated its supply chain data accuracy at a median of three out of five.
“Enforcement is no longer on the horizon. It is here. Border officials look at evidence to decide which goods move and which goods they hold,” said Shameek Ghosh, CEO and Co-Founder of TrusTrace.
Suppliers need clearer documentation guidance
Supplier resistance or limited capability was the most frequently cited barrier, named by 60% of respondents. Meanwhile, 63% identified industry-wide supplier data standards as a way to speed progress, making it the most selected option.
The report includes interviews with Brooks Running, a TrusTrace customer, and U.S. apparel group Komar. It also included Christian Hudson of the UN Center for Trade Facilitation and Julie Robertson of PIP Global Safety.
“The hardest part is that there is no single right answer for what a complete document set looks like at each level of the supply chain, which makes it genuinely difficult for suppliers to know how much is enough,” said Tahagod Mohamed, Senior Traceability Analyst at Brooks Running.
“Our guidance to them is simple: provide as much as you can to show how the raw material was produced, processed, transported , and paid for to make the final product,” Mohamed said.
The survey received 57 responses across 24 countries during the first half of 2026, including 40 fully completed surveys. Participants included sustainability directors, compliance leads, supply chain heads, and C-suite executives, along with a small number of manufacturers , mills and industry organizations. Percentages were calculated using only those who answered each question, with sample sizes ranging from 24 to 55.
Ways to improve readiness
The report outlines five stages for improving readiness: identify suppliers, trace materials back to their origin, connect information across company functions, automate compliance monitoring, and prepare documentation for review. The framework draws on practices from brands the report identifies as furthest ahead.
Its proposed 90-day agenda includes assessing how much reliable information a company holds at each supplier level, screening against entity lists, and testing whether it can assemble the documentation needed to respond to a CBP inquiry.

JPMorgan Chase & Co. headquarters in New York. ( Stock image by Katherine Welles. )
Posted By: Cecilia Jamasmie October 13, 2026
JPMorganChase (NYSE: JPM) has appointed Andrew Frame to lead critical minerals investment efforts under its $1.5-trillion (C$2.1 trillion) Security and Resiliency Initiative (SRI), placing him at the centre of a push to strengthen United States and allied supply chains for materials essential to manufacturing, energy and defence.
Frame will oversee the bank’s critical minerals strategy across extraction, refining and processing, identifying investment opportunities and addressing bottlenecks that threaten access to strategic resources. His mandate forms part of JPMorganChase’s 10-year initiative to facilitate financing and investment in industries considered vital to economic and national security.
“It has become painfully clear that the United States has allowed itself to become too reliant on unreliable sources of critical minerals, products and manufacturing—all of which are essential for our national security,” JPMorganChase chairman and CEO Jamie Dimon said when the initiative was announced.
Frame’s appointment comes as Western governments and companies seek to diversify mineral supplies and reduce their exposure to concentrated overseas production and processing capacity. Securing reliable sources of these materials has become increasingly important for defence systems, electric vehicles, renewable energy infrastructure and advanced technologies.
Priorities
JPMorganChase’s SRI targets four broad sectors: supply chains and advanced manufacturing, defence and aerospace, energy independence and resilience, and frontier technologies.
The bank has identified 27 subcategories within those sectors, including critical minerals, nuclear energy, battery storage, semiconductors, robotics and advanced defence components.
Critical minerals, pharmaceutical precursors and robotics fall under the manufacturing category, while defence investments will target autonomous systems, drones, secure communications and aerospace technologies.
Energy financing will include nuclear power, battery storage, distributed energy and electrical grid resilience. The technology portfolio will cover artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, quantum computing and other emerging industries, including semiconductors and nanomaterials.
The financing commitment involves facilitating and financing transactions for clients, with a separate $10-billion allocation earmarked for potential equity and venture capital investments.
Support expansion
JPMorganChase plans to recruit additional bankers, investment professionals and industry specialists to support the initiative. It will also establish an external advisory council comprising public- and private-sector leaders to help shape its long-term strategy.
The bank’s existing relationships could provide a broad platform for deploying capital. It serves 34,000 mid-sized companies and more than 90% of Fortune 500 businesses, alongside established private equity and venture capital partners.
Its Commercial & Investment Bank has held a leading position in global investment banking for more than 15 years, with experience financing and advising companies in defence, aerospace, healthcare and energy.
The initiative has drawn on research into private companies, rare earth supply chains and emerging technologies. JPMorganChase’s recently established Center for Geopolitics will provide analysis of international developments, while its Asset & Wealth Management division will contribute investment expertise.
Beyond financing, the bank intends to advocate for policies that encourage research and development, streamline permitting and procurement and reduce regulatory barriers. It also plans to work with business and community partners to strengthen workforce training in industries facing shortages of skilled labour.
Implementation will depend partly on the ability of companies to advance projects through permitting, secure qualified workers and establish commercially viable operations. The initiative sets out financing ambitions rather than guaranteed spending or completed investments.
“America needs more speed and investment,” Dimon said. “It also needs to remove obstacles that stand in the way: excessive regulations, bureaucratic delay, partisan gridlock and an education system not aligned to the skills we need.”

26 photos
Photo: eBay seller jabuc_25
The previous owner passed before finishing. This is how the current owner of this 1961 Ford Thunderbird describes the car, revealing that it’s a work in progress that has every part it needs in the trunk.
In other words, this 1961 Thunderbird is exactly what you need if you want an easy project. The car is already complete, so theoretically, someone with the right skills only needs to put it back together and bring the car to the road.
It’s not an easy project, though. It’s all because this T-Bird deserves the touch of a professional, especially as it seems to check all the boxes for a collectible.
First, it looks original. Second, it appears to be complete. Third, it has a fantastic number on the clock. Fourth, despite being described as a barn find, it’s running and driving.
Photo: eBay seller jabuc_25 Not many people remember this, but a Thunderbird convertible was chosen in 1961 to pace the Indianapolis 500. This helped the T-Bird gain more popularity, and this was more than welcome, especially considering the prices. It didn’t take long for the base Thunderbird to cost more than $5,000, so Ford had no option but to convince buyers that the car was worth the price.
“Here is the finest expression of the Thunderbird spirit, unquestionably Thunderbird in its classic lines and sparkling performance - not a hair wider nor a tenth of an inch longer - yet a Thunderbird so uniquely new that it stands alone in the fine-car field,” Ford said.
Ford used its booklets and marketing materials mostly to highlight the premium features on the T-Bird. One of them was the Swing-Away Steering Wheel.
“The steering wheel moves over to welcome you in,” Ford explained, revealing that the steering wheel could be moved for up to 10 inches to “take the driver’s seat easily.”
The Thunderbird was fitted with a 390 Special V8 paired with a new Cruise-O-Matic transmission, power steering, and power brakes. All these goodies were offered standard on every T-Bird sold this year.
Photo: eBay seller jabuc_25 That’s why this Ford Thunderbird should return to the road. It looks mostly original, and the engine under the hood is a correct 390. Unfortunately, the seller doesn’t share more specifics about the powertrain, but considering it’s a barn find that’s been sitting for quite a while, I would assume that it’s the original unit.
A quick inspection and a verification of the numbers should help any potential buyer figure out the whole story, so just call the seller and ask for additional data.
It’s unclear if the engine has already been rebuilt, but it starts and runs. It needs carb work, the seller reveals, so my recommendation is that you ask your mechanic to go there in person and see what they find under the hood.
The car also needs a brake booster, but a new one is in the trunk, along with all the other extras that might appear to be missing when you inspect the car digitally.
Photo: eBay seller jabuc_25 The metal looks fairly solid, which makes me think that the previous owner who started working on this Thunderbird was focused mostly on the metalwork. I would still check everything in person before making an offer, especially if the long-term objective is keeping this T-Bird original and returning it to the day-one configuration.
Look for patches under the car because a long time of sitting typically means that the floors are struggling with the invasion of rust. It’s unclear if the undersides have already been fixed or they didn’t require much work, but that’s what live inspections are for.
1961 Thunderbirds aren’t necessarily rare, so I think that the main selling point for this specimen is the number on the clock and how complete it continues to be after all these years. The odometer shows a little over 29K miles, and it’s safe to assume that this is the original mileage. However, I would still have this checked, especially if the goal is a complete restoration.
Photo: eBay seller jabuc_25 As for the price, I don’t think it’s necessarily ambitious, but considering 1961 Thunderbirds aren’t the most desirable, it looks like the car will have a hard time finding a new home.
The owner listed the car for auction, with the starting bid set at $5,000. A reserve is also in place, meaning that while you’ll have to bid $5,000 to join the digital fight, you’ll have to pay more to win it. I believe the reserve’s value is close to the BIN price, which is $7,000 for this auction.
Unsurprisingly, the auction is still at 0 bids, and there’s a chance the price is keeping people away for the time being. I still expect the car to sell eventually, but a no-reserve auction would have increased its chances to find a buyer on the first attempt.
The car is parked in Walnut, Grove, Missouri, and the auction is scheduled to end in 6 days.

Walmart ’s multibillion-dollar warehouse automation push is running into packaging problems, robot breakdowns and higher operating costs, according to a recent Wall Street Journal story . The retailer plans to replace shipping boxes that do not fit its automated systems, while some oversized products still require workers to handle them.
What’s Related
Walmart plans to replace boxes it has used for more than two decades with versions that are 1.5 inches shorter. The new boxes must be taped shut, adding work and expense, although Walmart says they will reduce shelf-stocking time at stores.
The transition involves most of Walmart’s roughly 200 U.S. supply chain buildings. Its warehouse operations rely on more than 140,000 workers to unload, sort, store and ship merchandise.
Rob Montgomery, Head of Supply Chain Operations for Walmart U.S., described the transition to the Journal: “We are kind of in this peak complexity.” He also said Walmart is changing its warehouses while keeping them operating, which adds to the difficulty.
RELATED STORIES : Walmart Ranks Third in Top 25 Supply Chain Rankings | Walmart to Pay Drivers $100 Million in Settlement Over Misleading Pay
Older warehouses making things complicated
Most of Walmart’s supply chain buildings date to the 1980s and ’90s, and about 80% of its automation construction projects are retrofits. Montgomery said Walmart is installing the equipment while keeping warehouses operating, which complicates the transition.
Different products also require different automated systems, often supplied by different companies. Some goods, including large-screen televisions and jumbo bags of dog food, will need manual assistance for the foreseeable future, Montgomery said.
Repairs and electricity add costs
Symbotic, the Massachusetts robotics company in which Walmart owns a 12.6% stake, supplies equipment that moves merchandise and builds pallets for shipment to stores. A company spokesman told the Journal that about 5% of its product-moving robots were undergoing repairs at any given time in recent months, down from under 10% last year.
Monthly electricity bills at Walmart’s automated grocery facilities can reach $800,000 or more during peak heating or cooling months, compared with roughly $250,000 under more manual operations, a person familiar with the situation told the Journal. The engineers needed to run the equipment also cost more than workers doing manual warehouse tasks, the Journal reported.
Despite those challenges, Walmart continues to expand its use of automation. By August, more than 65% of its stores were receiving some automated freight , and over 50% of its e-commerce inventory was moving through automated systems.
The retailer expects spending on store remodeling and supply chain automation to peak this year and next. Montgomery said top executives and the board view automation as a worthwhile long-term project despite the difficulties.
“We know that if we wait till perfect,” he told the Journal, “it’ll take too long.”

1973 Plymouth Duster 340 Six-Pack Is the One-of-Zero Hero Chrysler Never Had the Brass To Build

Photo: YouTube/CARFINDER
When gearheads discuss high-profile classic Mopar machines, names like Hemi winged warriors, the twin-cousin E-bodies Cuda and Challenger, Max Wedge Polaras and Savoys, letter car Chryslers, Crown Imperials, and De Soto Adventurers usually kickstart the conversation. The Plymouth Duster rarely enters this chat – but when it does, it slams the doors open with the force of a category Six hurricane. As in Six Barrels.
To set the record straight, we are not talking about standard grocery-getter models. The Duster 340 earned a reputation as a big-block slayer on streets and drag strips, unafraid to take on game much larger than itself.
A restored 1973 Plymouth Duster 340 surfaced at a classic car cruise night in San Diego, California, captured on the CARFINDER YouTube channel. While this Plymouth left the factory with a 340 V8, the owner added an upward deviation from factory specifications. The video highlights a six-barrel carburetor setup, an induction system Plymouth never officially offered on the entire 1973 Duster factory model lineup. Or on any Duster, period. Or on any other car post-1971.
To fit this induction setup, the owner installed a custom hood scoop, and retrofitted drag wheels for good measure – and good intentions. This six-barrel setup bridges the gap to the history of the Chrysler 340 V8. This powerhouse debuted in 1968 as a high-performance engine designed for high revolutions (pun intended).
Photo: YouTube/CARFINDER Chrysler engineered it from the ground up to rival the Chevrolet 350 and 302. The standard 4-barrel variant produced 275 horsepower, but Chrysler conservatively underrated these factory output power numbers.
The six-barrel variant of this engine achieved historical status. The 340 V8 received three two-barrel carburetors for the 1970 model year, a setup was introduced to meet homologation requirements for SCCA Trans-Am racing. Chrysler bolted this induction system onto modified engine blocks featuring thicker webs, unleashing 290 horsepower and 345 pound-feet of torque. The NHRA rated this engine much higher, placing it in the 320 to 330 horsepower racing class.
Photo: YouTube/CARFINDER This six-barrel configuration found its way into only two cars. Dodge received it for the Challenger T/A, and Plymouth fitted it to the AAR Cuda. Production numbers were limited, with 2,399 units built for the Challenger T/A and 2,724 units for the AAR Cuda. By 1971, the six-barrel setup vanished. The standard four-barrel 340 powered Chrysler products until it went out of production after the 1973 model year concluded.
Federal emissions regulations and lowered compression ratios sapped the engine of its power. Plymouth replaced the 340 with the larger 360 V8 in 1974. The 360 offered more torque but lacked the high-revving soul of its predecessor. The 1973 Duster 340 represented the final chapter for this engine.
The Plymouth Duster itself has a documented history, with production spanning continuously from 1970 through 1976. It remained a single generation vehicle platform, introduced to replace the A-body Valiant, and to fill the void left in the segment by the Barracuda’s promotion to the E-body platform.
Photo: YouTube/CARFINDER The Duster was built upon the Valiant compact platform – in fact, at its birth, it was dubbed Valiant Duster, for one year only. Plymouth designers received a budget of 15,000,000 dollars to create a different exterior look.
They retained the Valiant front end and crafted a semi-fastback rear. Enthusiasts cite 1970 as the best year of production for the Duster. This inaugural year introduced the factory visual expression of the car, free from crash bumpers that plagued later production model year body design iterations.
The engines and transmissions available that year offered something for every buyer. Economy drivers opted for the 198 cubic-inch or 225 cubic-inch Slant Sixes. Drivers seeking more vigor chose the 318 V8 or gravitated toward the top-tier 340 V8. Buyers paired these powerplants with a 3-speed manual, a 4-speed manual, or a 3-speed Torqueflite automatic transmission . Competitive base pricing proved to be the key to the overall sales success story.
Photo: YouTube/CARFINDER The factory base price for the cheapest 1970 Duster with the inline 6 was 2,172 dollars. The 340 model began at 2,547 dollars. Adding the Torqueflite automatic transmission increased the base price for a 340 automatic to 2,760 dollars. This affordability allowed Plymouth to sell 217,192 units in 1970. In 1971, production hit 186,478 units. By 1972, it surged to 228,022 units. The Duster remained a sales juggernaut during the 1973 model year.
Plymouth sold 248,105 Dusters in 1973. Out of those, 15,731 were Duster 340 models, out of the total production for Chrysler vehicles equipped with the 340 V8 of 51,067 units. This was the second-best year for the engine, trailing the 56,672 record achieved in 1970. Most of the 340 models sold in 1973 were automatics, with 8,312 receiving a Torqueflite. Just 2,037 models featured a 4-speed manual gearbox.
The standard 3-speed manual transmission came in 1,492 examples. The math doesn’t add up, does it (pun premeditated)? The total “shipped to US dealers” Duster 340s went as high as 11,841 units – according to Galen Govier’s White Book.
Photo: YouTube/CARFINDER The reliable Torqueflite automatic was the preferred choice for drag racing, which brings us back to the green 1973 Duster captured by CARFINDER, a tribute to Mopar history. The owner did not stick to factory specifications, choosing to graft the six-barrel setup onto the A-body. This created a lightweight machine that Chrysler never built, righting a historical wrong done over half a century ago.
Since the owner was absent when the video was filmed, the exact power output remains unknown. The large hood scoop and the wide rear tires suggest the vehicle frequents the quarter-mile. A well-tuned Duster 340 could embarrass big-block cars at the stoplight drags due to its lightweight chassis. It weighed significantly less than a GTO or a Challenger R/T, operating as the ultimate street-sleeper nose-bleeder.

BMW revamps the iX1 with Neue Klasse style
BMW introduced the iX1 in 2022 as its smallest, most affordable electric SUV. As part of its revamped lineup, BMW’s entry-level EV is due for an overhaul.
The next-gen iX1 will be one of 40 new or refreshed models that BMW plans to launch through 2027, updated with its Neue Klasse design and technology.
While automakers traditionally introduce a mid-cycle facelift, BMW appears to be moving straight to a second-generation model built on the Neue Klasse EV platform.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
A camouflaged iX1 prototype was spotted racing around the Nürburgring by @Wilco blok , offering a sneak peek at the new design. Although it’s still disguised, it appears to adopt BMW’s new “Face,” trading its traditional oversized Kidney Grille for a slimmer, minimalist look.
From what’s shown, the new iX1 essentially looks like a baby iX3, moving away from its current ICE-derived design.
View this post on Instagram A post shared by ᴡɪʟᴄᴏ ʙʟᴏᴋ (@wilcoblok)
The new iX1 will also use BMW’s dedicated Neue Klasse EV platform, rather than the current platform it shares with the gas-powered X1.
As such, it will offer significant improvements in driving range, efficiency, and charging speeds. BMW introduced the 2026 iX1 eDrive20 and iX1 xDrive30 earlier this year with WLTP ranges of up to 512 km (318 miles) and 417 km (259 miles), respectively.
The interior will get a Neue Klasse overhaul, bringing more advanced tech, software, and plenty of digital screens.
BMW iX3 50 xDrive interior (Source: BMW)
BMW’s Neue Klasse interior setup includes a 17.9″ central touchscreen, a newly designed steering wheel, and its Panoramic Vision 3D Head-Up Display that stretches across the dashboard.
During its Capital Market Day on September 29, BMW revealed plans to launch a new fully electric entry-level model from the Neue Klasse in 2028. The new entry-level EV is expected to arrive as the i1, a sedan sibling to the iX1.
BMW has no plans to bring the iX1 to the US, but the new 2027 iX3 and i3 are now on sale, starting at $61,500 each.

New EVs still cost less than they did a year ago, but September brought buyers a double hit: higher prices and smaller discounts.
The average transaction price (ATP) paid for a new EV in the US rose to $55,879 in September, according to Kelley Blue Book, a Cox Automotive brand. That’s up about 2.4% from August’s downwardly revised average of $54,574.
Compared with September last year, though, EV prices were down 3%. Kelley Blue Book says a stronger mix of more affordable models helped lower the average.
So the longer-term picture is improving, even if September wasn’t a great month for bargain hunters.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The price premium for an EV over what Kelley Blue Book calls an “ICE+” model was 11% in September. That gap has stayed near 11% throughout 2026, down from an average of nearly 18% in 2025.
EV discounts are shrinking
Automakers also pulled back on EV incentives. Discounts averaged 11% of the ATP in September – their lowest level this year and down from 14.2% a year earlier. (September 2025 was the last month before the $7,500 federal tax credit expired, so there were some great incentives on the table.)
At September’s average EV price, that works out to roughly $6,147 in incentives. That’s an industry average, so the actual offer will depend on the vehicle you’re shopping for. (The Polestar 4 , pictured above, has a rebate of up to $25,000 off its MSRP of $56,400 to $57,800, until November 2.)
Across the broader new-vehicle market, average transaction prices rose for the fourth consecutive month.
Tesla prices rose as well
Tesla’s ATP increased 3.3% month over month to $54,345 in September. Year over year, it barely changed, up 0.4%.
The Model 3 and Model Y accounted for nearly 97% of Tesla’s sales. Buyers paid an average of $53,804 for the Model 3 and $53,052 for the Model Y.
Nearly 1,500 Cybertrucks sold in September, with an average transaction price of $98,109.
For EV shoppers, the gap with ICE vehicles has narrowed considerably since 2025. But September’s higher prices and smaller incentives show that cheaper EV prices aren’t arriving in a straightforward way.
